It explains round-trip time (RTT), the delay×bandwidth product, and illustrates how latency or bandwidth dominates performance for different object sizes and network conditions, including examples like a 1-byte message versus a 25-MB image transfer. It also discusses the concept of instructions per mile.

nodes.title: 1.5.2 Delay X Bandwidth Product
nodes.summary: The text covers network performance metrics, including a figure showing perceived latency vs. RTT for different object sizes and link speeds, and an example of instruction cost per mile. It explains the delay × bandwidth product as the volume of a pipe, its importance for high-performance networks, and provides examples. It clarifies bit/byte and kilo/mega definitions, giving conversion approximations. It includes a table of sample delay × bandwidth products. Finally, it discusses high-speed networks, noting that latency does not improve with bandwidth due to the speed of light, and illustrates the difference in transmitting a 1-MB file over 1-Mbps vs. 1-Gbps links.

nodes.title: 1.5.3 High-Speed Networks
nodes.summary: The text covers network performance topics: Table 1.1 shows delay × bandwidth products for various links. Section 1.5.3 discusses high-speed networks, noting bandwidth increases but latency (speed of light) remains fixed, with examples comparing 1-MB file transfer over 1-Mbps vs 1-Gbps links. It explains the delay × bandwidth product and effective throughput formula (TransferTime = RTT + 1/Bandwidth × TransferSize), showing how RTT limits throughput. Section 1.5.4 addresses application performance needs, noting some applications like video have upper bandwidth limits, illustrated with a video streaming example requiring 75 Mbps.

nodes.title: 1.5.4 Application Performance Needs
nodes.summary: The text covers network performance, effective throughput, and application needs. It calculates effective throughput for a 1-MB file transfer over a 1-Gbps network with 100 ms RTT, showing 74.1 Mbps due to latency, and notes larger transfers improve efficiency while retransmissions hurt small transfers. It contrasts network-centric performance with application-specific needs, like video requiring 75 Mbps but having variable compressed rates, and discusses bursts, buffering, and jitter from variable latency, emphasizing bounds and buffering to smooth playback.

nodes.title: 1.6 Summary
nodes.summary: The text explains network-induced jitter, its cause from variable queuing delays in multihop networks, and its impact on video streaming, noting that buffering can smooth jitter if latency bounds are known. It then summarizes Chapter 1: the goal of building a functional network, requirements for scalable connectivity via packet switching, layered architectures (OSI and Internet), protocol implementation using sockets, and performance metrics of latency and throughput, including delay × bandwidth product. It concludes with the Internet's growth, diverse players, and the future of cloud computing, ubiquitous mobile access, and large-scale data centers.

nodes.title: What’s Next: Cloud Computing
nodes.summary: The text summarizes computer networks' evolution from ARPANET to pervasive systems involving industry, telecom, and entrepreneurs creating Internet services like VOIP and cloud computing (e.g., Amazon). It highlights ubiquitous networking across mobile devices and sensors, the need for scalable, mobile-friendly Internet, and reliance on large data centers. It lists technical challenges (connectivity, security, etc.) and states the book's focus. Further reading cites references on telecommunication history, Internet architecture, end-to-end argument, and RISC systems approach.

nodes.title: Further Reading

nodes.title: Exercises

nodes.title: Problem: Connecting To A Network
nodes.summary: The text introduces the problem of connecting nodes to networks, starting with a Winston Churchill quote. It discusses the need for a physical medium and outlines five key issues: encoding bits, framing, error detection, reliable delivery, and media access control. It then applies these issues to three network technologies: point-to-point links, CSMA networks like Ethernet, and wireless networks like 802.11, aiming to survey technology and explore fundamental link problems for building scalable networks.

2.1 Perspectives on connecting (intro)
nodes.summary: This chapter section discusses connecting nodes via links, covering five key problems: encoding bits, framing, error detection, reliable delivery, and media access control. nodes.title: 2.3 Framing
2.3 Framing (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers Manchester encoding's 50% efficiency due to doubled signal transition rate (baud rate), and 4B/5B encoding which inserts extra bits to avoid long runs of 0s, achieving 80% efficiency. It details 5-bit code rules, unused codes for idle, dead, halt, and control symbols, with a reference to Table 2.2. Framing is introduced for packet-switched networks, where adaptors exchange frames and must determine frame boundaries. Byte-oriented protocols (BISYNC, PPP, DDCMP) are discussed, focusing on sentinel characters (SYN, STX, ETX) and DLE escaping in BISYNC.

nodes.title: Sentinel-Based Approaches
nodes.summary: The text discusses framing in data communication, starting with bits flowing between adaptors and frames between hosts. It covers byte-oriented protocols BISYNC, PPP, and DDCMP. BISYNC uses sentinel characters (SYN, STX, ETX) and character stuffing with DLE escaping, plus CRC for error detection and header fields. PPP similarly uses sentinels and character stuffing, with negotiated fields via LCP. DDCMP uses a byte-counting approach with a COUNT field. The text also mentions bit-oriented protocols like HDLC, which view frames as bits.

nodes.title: Byte-Counting Approach
nodes.summary: The text presents PPP and DDCMP frame formats, then explains byte-counting framing where a COUNT field in the header specifies the frame body's byte length, as used by DECNET's DDCMP. It notes a risk: transmission errors corrupting the COUNT can cause framing errors, where the receiver misidentifies frame end, though error detection catches the bad frame; the receiver then waits for the next SYN to resynchronize, potentially causing back-to-back frames to be incorrectly received. It contrasts byte-oriented protocols with bit-oriented protocols like HDLC, which ignore byte boundaries and treat frames as bit collections from various data types.

nodes.title: 2.3.2 Bit-Oriented Protocols (HDLC)
nodes.summary: The text covers framing in data link protocols: byte-counting approach (e.g., DDCMP) where a count field risks framing errors requiring resynchronization via SYN; bit-oriented protocols (HDLC) using bit stuffing with 01111110 flags, where five 1s trigger stuffing/removal, and errors discard frames; a discussion on protocol layering and layer violations; and clock-based framing (SONET) using fixed 810-byte frames with overhead and a repeating pattern, avoiding bit stuffing and supporting multiplexing.

nodes.title: 2.3.3 Clock-Based Framing (SONET)
nodes.summary: This text discusses clock-based framing using SONET, covering its origin, dominance, and scope, including framing, encoding, and multiplexing. It details STS-1 frame structure, synchronization without bit stuffing, NRZ encoding, and payload scrambling for clock recovery. SONET supports multiplexing via STS-N rates, byte interleaving, concatenation (STS-Nc), and floating payloads. The section concludes by introducing error detection, its importance, historical codes like Hamming and Reed-Solomon, and basic error handling approaches.

Byte-oriented protocols (BISYNC, PPP, DDCMP) are detailed, including sentinel-based approaches with SYN, STX, ETX, DLE escaping, and character stuffing; byte-counting with a COUNT field and its corruption risks; and bit-oriented protocols like HDLC using bit stuffing with 01111110 flags. nodes.title: 2.4 Error Detection
2.4 Error Detection (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers SONET frame payload floating and shifting with overhead pointing to payload start for clock synchronization. It introduces error detection, discussing bit errors, retransmission vs. error-correcting codes, and defines redundant bits, error-detecting codes, and checksums. It mentions Hamming and Reed-Solomon codes and notes CRC use in link-level protocols. It describes two-dimensional parity, explaining one-dimensional parity and how two-dimensional parity adds a parity byte, catching 1-, 2-, and 3-bit errors and most 4-bit errors.

nodes.title: 2.4.1 Two-Dimensional Parity
nodes.summary: The text discusses error detection using redundant bits derived from the message via a shared algorithm, which the receiver verifies. It defines error-detecting codes and checksums, noting terminology misuse. Two-dimensional parity is explained, which adds parity bits per byte and a parity byte for the frame, catching 1-, 2-, 3-bit, and most 4-bit errors. The Internet checksum is described, which sums 16-bit words using ones complement arithmetic, takes the ones complement, and verifies at the receiver. It is not used at the link level but provides similar functionality.

nodes.title: 2.4.2 Internet Checksum Algorithm
nodes.summary: The text covers error detection techniques: two-dimensional parity with a 42-bit message and 14 redundant bits; the Internet checksum algorithm, including ones complement arithmetic, a code example, and its trade-offs; simple probability estimates for network errors with examples; and an introduction to Cyclic Redundancy Checks (CRCs), explaining polynomial representation of messages and the use of a divisor polynomial.

nodes.title: 2.4.3 Cyclic Redundancy Check
nodes.summary: The text explains Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) for error detection: representing messages as polynomials, using a divisor polynomial C(x), polynomial arithmetic modulo 2, and the steps to compute CRC (multiply by x^k, divide, subtract remainder). It details error detection properties for single-bit, double-bit, odd, and burst errors, and lists common CRC polynomials used in protocols like Ethernet and HDLC. It also discusses hardware implementation with shift registers and XOR gates, compares error detection versus correction (FEC), and notes trade-offs and applications.

Finally, it explains Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC), covering polynomial representation, modulo 2 arithmetic, computation steps, error detection properties for various error types, common CRC polynomials, hardware implementation, and comparison with forward error correction.

nodes.title: 2.5 Reliable Transmission
2.5 Reliable Transmission (intro)
nodes.summary: This text covers CRC polynomials (common types and calculation using shift registers), reliable transmission, and ARQ mechanisms. It explains error detection with CRC and the need to recover lost frames at the link level or higher layers. It introduces acknowledgments (ACKs), timeouts, and automatic repeat request (ARQ), then describes the stop-and-wait ARQ algorithm where the sender waits for an ACK before sending the next frame and retransmits on timeout.

nodes.title: 2.5.1 Stop-and-Wait
nodes.summary: This text covers reliable transmission at the link layer, noting that errors require frame recovery via acknowledgments and timeouts, forming Automatic Repeat Request (ARQ). It acknowledges reliability may be provided at higher layers. It details the stop-and-wait ARQ algorithm, including its operation, four timeline scenarios (success, lost frame, lost ACK, premature timeout), duplicate frame issues solved by 1-bit sequence numbers, and its inefficiency due to allowing only one outstanding frame, limiting throughput below link capacity. The concept of delay × bandwidth product and keeping the pipe full is introduced, leading to sliding window as a solution.

nodes.title: 2.5.2 Sliding Window
2.5.2 Sliding Window (intro)
nodes.summary: This text explains stop-and-wait's limitation of low throughput, using a 1-bit sequence number example with a 182 kbps max rate. It introduces the delay × bandwidth product concept to keep the pipe full. The sliding window algorithm is then detailed: the sender assigns sequence numbers (SeqNum), maintains send window size (SWS), last acknowledgment received (LAR), and last frame sent (LFS) with invariant LFS - LAR ≤ SWS, retransmits on timer expiration, and buffers up to SWS frames. The receiver maintains receive window size (RWS), largest acceptable frame (LAF), and last frame received (LFR), also referencing Figure 2.20.

nodes.title: The Sliding Window Algorithm
nodes.summary: The text explains the sliding window algorithm for reliable transmission. It details sender and receiver variables (SWS, LAR, LFS, RWS, LAF, LFR), invariants, and the process of accepting frames, sending cumulative acknowledgments, and handling out-of-order frames. It discusses timeouts, retransmissions, and performance issues like decreasing in-transit data during packet loss. It also covers negative and selective acknowledgments, and the impact of finite sequence numbers, including wrap-around and the constraint SWS < (MaxSeqNum + 1)/2 when RWS = SWS.

nodes.title: Finite Sequence Numbers and Sliding Window
nodes.summary: This text discusses sliding window protocol details: it explains finite sequence numbers wrapping around, the constraint that MaxSeqNum must exceed outstanding frames, and the condition SWS < (MaxSeqNum + 1)/2 when RWS = SWS, illustrating with a lost ACK example. It notes the rule assumes no frame reordering, which may not hold in other environments. It then introduces the Sliding Window Protocol (SWP) implementation, defining the protocol layers HLP and LLP, and presents data structures including the frame header (SeqNum, AckNum, Flags) and sending-side state with LAR, LFS, sendQ, and sendWindowNotFull.

nodes.title: Implementation of Sliding Window
nodes.summary: The text covers the sliding window algorithm's implementation in the Sliding Window Protocol (SWP), including data structures (frame header, sender/receiver state), routines sendSWP and deliverSWP, and the swpInWindow helper. It explains semaphore use, window size rules, sequence number space assumptions, and cumulative ACKs. It also discusses the algorithm's three roles: reliable transmission, frame order preservation, and flow control, noting that order preservation may be optional depending on network architecture.

nodes.title: Frame Order and Flow Control
nodes.summary: This text discusses the sliding window protocol's three roles: reliable delivery, preserving frame order, and flow control. It explains how receivers buffer out-of-order frames and how flow control throttles senders via buffer space feedback. Emphasizing separation of concerns, it questions whether combining these functions at the link level is effective, noting the protocol is revisited in later chapters. It then introduces ARPANET's concurrent logical channels, which multiplex multiple logical channels over a link using stop-and-wait on each, allowing full link utilization without ordering or flow control, with 8 channels on ground links and 16 on satellite links.

nodes.title: 2.5.3 Concurrent Logical Channels

nodes.title: 2.6 Ethernet and Multiple Access Networks (802.3)
2.6 Ethernet and Multiple Access Networks (802.3) (intro)
nodes.summary: This text discusses Ethernet and multiple access networks (802.3), covering the evolution of Ethernet from Xerox PARC as the dominant LAN technology using CSMA/CD, its roots in the Aloha network, and the shift from shared coaxial cable to point-to-point links while multi-access principles now apply to wireless networks. nodes.title: 2.6.1 Physical Properties
nodes.summary: This text covers Ethernet fundamentals, including its history from the 1978 DEC-Intel-Xerox 10-Mbps standard to IEEE 802.3 and higher speeds. It details physical properties: original coaxial cable up to 500m with taps, transceivers, and adaptors; modern twisted pair or fiber. It explains repeaters, hubs, and terminators, noting broadcast signals, collision domains, and encoding schemes. nodes.title: 2.6.2 Access Protocol
Frame Format

Key points include the 1500-byte max data, 46-byte minimum for collision detection, and 14-byte header, emphasizing bit-oriented framing and hardware implementation of the algorithm.

nodes.title: Addresses
nodes.summary: The text covers Ethernet (802.3) frame format, including preamble, addresses, type, body, and CRC, noting a 14-byte header. Finally, it describes the transmitter algorithm: 1-persistent protocol, immediate transmission when idle or after busy line becomes idle, and the 9.6 μs interframe gap.

nodes.title: Transmitter Algorithm
nodes.summary: The text covers Ethernet multicast addressing and receiver acceptance rules (own, broadcast, multicast, promiscuous). It details the transmitter algorithm: immediate transmission when idle, 1-persistent protocol, and p-persistent alternatives with slotted Aloha. Finally, practical experience notes Ethernets perform best under light loads, with typical deployments using fewer hosts and shorter cables than the standard allows.

nodes.title: 2.6.3 Experience with Ethernet

Success factors include easy administration, low cost, and eventual shift to switched Ethernet. nodes.title: 2.7 Wireless
2.7 Wireless (intro)

nodes.title: Token Rings

nodes.title: 2.7.1 802.11/Wi-Fi
Physical Properties
nodes.summary: Section 2.7 covers wireless networking, specifically IEEE 802.11/Wi-Fi. nodes.title: Collision Avoidance
nodes.summary: This text covers 802.11 wireless networking: support for multiple standards (a, b, g, n) with varying bit rates and modulation/error-correcting codes; bit rate selection based on noise, using SNR measurement or probing; collision avoidance (CSMA/CA) with ACKs and optional RTS-CTS to address hidden and exposed node problems; exponential backoff for collisions; and base-station-oriented topology with access points connected via a link-layer distribution system, enabling node association and roaming.

nodes.title: Distribution System
nodes.summary: The text covers 802.11 wireless networks: RTS/CTS collision handling and exponential backoff; distribution systems with access points (APs) and link-layer connections; node association via active scanning (Probe, Association Request/Response) and passive scanning (Beacon frames); AP switching due to mobility; and the 802.11 frame format with source/destination addresses, data, CRC, Control field, and four address fields including ToDS/FromDS.

nodes.title: Frame Format
nodes.summary: This text covers IEEE 802.11 wireless LAN operations and frame format, plus Bluetooth (802.15.1). It describes node mobility between APs using active scanning (Probe/Probe Response) and passive scanning (Beacon/Association Request). nodes.title: 2.7.2 Bluetooth® (802.15.1)
nodes.summary: The text first explains IEEE 802.11 frame addressing, detailing Addr1–Addr4 roles depending on ToDS/FromDS bits, with a direct-send versus distribution-system forwarding example.
