nodes.title: 2.7.3 Cell Phone Technologies
nodes.summary: The text covers wireless networking: Bluetooth piconets with master/slave roles and parked/active states; sensors as cheap networked devices for monitoring; cell phone technologies including licensed spectrum, global frequency variations, multiple standards, base stations, cells, handoffs, and generations (1G analog, 2G digital data, 3G broadband, 4G emerging) with CDMA as a key 3G spread-spectrum multiplexing technique; cross-layer issues where wireless link information is passed to higher layers to improve performance, challenging strict layering; security concerns for wireless links including privacy, unauthorized access, and access control mechanisms, with details in Chapter 8; and satellite communications for phones and broadcasting, limited by cost and size.

The section covers wireless networking fundamentals, contrasting Ethernet's success and token ring's decline. It categorizes wireless technologies by data rate, range, spectrum, and licensing, then details IEEE 802.11/Wi-Fi (physical layers, CSMA/CA, frame formats, topologies, mobility), Bluetooth (piconets, frequency hopping, low power), ZigBee for sensors, and cell phone technologies (generations, CDMA, handoffs). It also addresses spectrum sharing, spread spectrum, cross-layer issues, security concerns, and satellite communications.

nodes.title: 2.8 Summary
nodes.summary: The text discusses wireless network privacy risks, unauthorized data injection, and access control mechanisms leading to wireless security. It covers satellite communications, including satphones and broadcasting. The chapter summary reviews link types and five key problems: encoding (NRZ, NRZI, Manchester, 4B/5B), framing (byte-oriented, bit-oriented, clock-based), error detection (CRC, two-dimensional parity, checksums), ARQ for reliable links (stop-and-wait, sliding window, concurrent channels), and multiple-access protocols for shared links (Ethernet, wireless, hidden nodes, mesh networks). It also introduces the Internet of Things, smart grids, and networking everyday appliances for energy control.

nodes.title: What’s Next: “The Internet Of Things”
nodes.summary: The text discusses wireless LAN media access challenges like hidden nodes and base-station vs. mesh networks. It traces the Internet host evolution from fixed computers to mobile devices and now small sensors/actuators, introducing the Internet of Things. Practical applications include smart grids for energy control via sensors and actuators. Technical challenges involve IPv6 addressing, new routing protocols for low-power unreliable devices, and specialized operating systems. The vision's outcome remains uncertain but signals the Internet moving beyond computer interconnection. Further reading lists key papers on Ethernet and wireless MAC protocols, and notes textbooks on telecommunications-focused networking.

nodes.title: Further Reading
nodes.summary: The text covers technical challenges of pushing networking to trillions of small, low-power, intermittently connected devices, including IPv6 address scaling, energy-efficient routing, and specialized operating systems for the Internet of Things. It lists further readings on Ethernet, wireless networks, sensor networking, information theory, error codes, and CRCs. Finally, it presents five exercises on line encoding (NRZ, Manchester, NRZI), 4B/5B encoding, code constraints, and bit stuffing.

nodes.title: Exercises
nodes.summary: This text presents 57 exercises covering data encoding (NRZ, Manchester, NRZI, 4B/5B), framing (bit stuffing, BISYNC, HDLC), error detection (two-dimensional parity, Internet checksum, CRC), and ARQ/sliding window protocols (stop-and-wait, selective ACKs, sequence numbers, flow control). It also includes Ethernet topics (propagation delay, minimum packet size, exponential backoff, capture effect, address collisions, simulation), wireless issues (hidden terminals, collision detection, mesh networks, sensor localization), and an introduction to internetworking and switches.

summary: Chapter 2 covers connecting nodes to networks, focusing on five key issues: encoding, framing, error detection, reliable delivery, and media access control. It examines point-to-point links, CSMA networks (Ethernet), and wireless (802.11), discussing link capacity, encoding schemes, framing methods (byte-oriented, bit-oriented, clock-based), error detection (parity, checksums, CRC), and reliable transmission via ARQ (stop-and-wait, sliding window). Ethernet's evolution and CSMA/CD are detailed, along with wireless technologies (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, ZigBee, cellular). The chapter concludes with the Internet of Things, further reading, and 57 exercises covering these topics.

title: Chapter 3. Internetworking

nodes.title: Problem: Not All Networks are Directly Connected
nodes.summary: The text introduces internetworking: interconnecting diverse networks to build a global network, as with the Internet. It outlines subproblems: switches/bridges link similar links, forwarding packets via connectionless or connection-oriented methods; routers, using IP, handle heterogeneity; routing finds efficient, loop-free, adaptive paths; and switch/router design ranges from general-purpose computers to specialized high-end routers. Section 3.1 begins with switching and bridging, defining a switch as a multi-input, multi-output device, adding star topology, and noting scalability by interconnecting multiple switches.

nodes.title: 3.1 Switching and bridging
3.1 Switching and bridging (intro)
nodes.summary: This text covers switched LANs, including switching and bridging concepts. It explains switch functions, star topology benefits, and scalability. It describes how switches forward packets using headers, comparing datagram (connectionless), virtual circuit (connection-oriented), and source routing approaches. It discusses node addresses and port identification. It also introduces routers for internetworking heterogeneous networks via IP, routing challenges (efficiency, loop-free, dynamic), and switch/router design, especially high-end specialized routers. Finally, it details datagram forwarding with an example forwarding table.

nodes.title: 3.1.1 Datagrams
nodes.summary: This text covers network layer switching in OSI, focusing on how switches decide packet output links by examining headers. It discusses three approaches: datagrams (connectionless), virtual circuits (connection-oriented), and source routing. It explains the need for globally unique end node addresses, using Ethernet as an example, and port identification via numbering or node names. Datagram forwarding uses complete destination addresses and forwarding tables, with characteristics like connectionless operation, independent packet forwarding, and robustness to failures. Virtual circuit switching is introduced as an alternative technique.

nodes.title: 3.1.2 Virtual Circuit Switching
3.1.2 Virtual Circuit Switching (intro)
3.1.2 Virtual Circuit Switching (intro)
nodes.summary: This text contrasts datagram and virtual circuit (VC) packet switching. It details datagram characteristics: connectionless, independent packet forwarding, and robustness to failures. It then explains VC switching: connection setup, VC tables, VCIs, permanent vs. switched VCs, signalling, data transfer, and teardown. It notes VC delays, reduced per-packet overhead, and failure impacts. It discusses resource allocation, hop-by-hop flow control, quality of service, and congestion, comparing VC (X.25) and datagram approaches. It concludes with VC technology examples (X.25, Frame Relay, ATM) and VPNs.

nodes.title: Introduction to Congestion
nodes.summary: The text introduces congestion in internetworking, distinguishing it from contention and discussing how virtual circuits (e.g., X.25) avoid congestion by preallocating buffers, while datagrams invite congestion but may achieve better utilization. It notes virtual circuit technologies like X.25, Frame Relay, and ATM, and their use in VPNs, now largely replaced by Internet technologies. It then covers optical switching, explaining factors like DWDM and optical amplifiers that enabled high-capacity optical networks, and describes optical switches that electronically cross-connect SONET channels, providing real circuits rather than virtual circuits.

nodes.title: Optical Switching
nodes.summary: The text covers optical switching, explaining its rise due to DWDM and optical amplifiers, enabling high-capacity networks. Optical switches, often electronic internally, cross-connect SONET channels, providing real circuits, with newer MEMS-based switches offering all-optical paths. It notes optical networks as infrastructure for SONET links and relevance to routing and MPLS. It then introduces ATM as a well-known virtual circuit technology, popular in the 1980s-90s, embraced by telephone companies, competing with Ethernet and IP. The ATM cell format is described, focusing on the 24-bit VPI/VCI fields, omitting the GFC bits.

nodes.title: Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM)
nodes.summary: The text covers optical switches using MEMS mirrors for uninterrupted optical channels, noting limited optical networking coverage and its role in SONET links, with routing protocols and MPLS applying to optical networking. It then discusses ATM as a well-known virtual circuit technology, its prominence in the 1980s-90s due to telephone industry adoption and high-speed switching needs, competition with Ethernet and IP, and examines the ATM cell format, including VPI, VCI, and other fields.

This section contrasts datagram and virtual circuit (VC) packet switching, detailing datagram characteristics (connectionless, independent forwarding, robustness) and VC operations (setup, tables, VCIs, permanent/switched VCs, signalling, data transfer, teardown). It discusses VC delays, overhead, failure impacts, resource allocation, flow control, QoS, and congestion, comparing VC (X.25) and datagram approaches. It introduces congestion in internetworking, noting VC preallocation avoids congestion while datagrams may achieve better utilization. It covers optical switching, driven by DWDM and amplifiers, including optical switches and MEMS-based all-optical paths, and their role in SONET and MPLS. It introduces ATM as a prominent VC technology, its competition with Ethernet/IP, and the ATM cell format (VPI/VCI fields). VC technology examples include X.25, Frame Relay, ATM, and VPNs.

nodes.title: Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM)
nodes.summary: The text covers optical networking using MEMS switches, noting limited coverage but relevance to routing protocols and MPLS. It then details ATM as a virtual circuit technology: its history, competition with Ethernet and IP, and cell format (VPI, VCI, HEC). It explains the rationale for fixed 53-byte cells—hardware simplicity and parallelism for scalability—and the trade-offs in cell size, including padding inefficiency and the 'cell tax,' with 48-byte payload as a compromise. Finally, it introduces source routing, where the source provides all topology information in the packet header, and describes a simple port-number-based switching implementation.

This section contrasts datagram and virtual circuit (VC) packet switching, covering datagram characteristics (connectionless forwarding, robustness) and VC operations (setup, tables, VCIs, permanent/switched VCs, signalling, data transfer, teardown). It discusses VC delays, overhead, failure impacts, resource allocation, flow control, QoS, and congestion, comparing VC (X.25) and datagram approaches, including congestion in internetworking. It covers optical switching (DWDM, amplifiers, MEMS-based all-optical paths) and its role in SONET and MPLS. It introduces ATM as a prominent VC technology, its competition with Ethernet/IP, and the ATM cell format (VPI/VCI fields), explaining the rationale for fixed 53-byte cells, trade-offs in cell size, padding inefficiency, and the 'cell tax.' VC technology examples include X.25, Frame Relay, ATM, and VPNs. It also introduces source routing and a port-number-based switching implementation.

nodes.title: 3.1.3 Source Routing
nodes.summary: The text discusses cell size trade-offs in ATM, noting that short cells increase header overhead and reduce data throughput, while long cells cause padding inefficiency known as the 'cell tax'; 48 bytes was a compromise. It then explains source routing, where the source host specifies the path via a list of switch ports, detailing rotation, stripping, and pointer header methods, their issues with variable header length, and their use in datagram and virtual circuit networks, including strict versus loose source routes. Finally, it introduces bridges and LAN switches, including VLANs (Lab 04).

nodes.title: 3.1.4 Bridges and LAN Switches
3.1.4 Bridges and LAN Switches (intro)
nodes.summary: This text covers source routing methods (rotation, stripping, pointer) for header handling, its use in datagram and virtual circuit networks, and strict vs. loose source routes. It introduces bridges and LAN switches for interconnecting Ethernets, explaining their operation, differences from repeaters, extended LANs, and bandwidth benefits. It also begins discussing learning bridges and their frame forwarding optimization.

nodes.title: Learning Bridges
nodes.summary: This text covers network bridging, including limitations of repeaters and the need for bridges to interconnect Ethernets. It explains bridge operation in promiscuous mode, extended LAN formation, and simple forwarding. It details learning bridges, which inspect source addresses to build forwarding tables, with timeouts and flooding for unknown destinations. It includes an illustration (Figure 3.9) and a forwarding table example (Table 3.4). It also discusses implementation with code structures (BridgeEntry, Map, MAX_TTL) and constants (BRIDGE_TAB_SIZE, MAX_TTL). Additionally, it notes bridges as switches that increase total bandwidth.

nodes.title: Implementation
nodes.summary: The text explains how a bridge learns addresses by inspecting source addresses to build a forwarding table, implementing connectionless datagram forwarding. Initially empty, the table adds entries with timeouts, and unknown destinations are flooded. Implementation details include the BridgeEntry structure, a map-based table, MAX_TTL, and the updateTable routine. Table-full handling involves dropping new entries. Finally, the spanning tree algorithm is introduced to prevent loops in extended LANs, which otherwise cause frames to loop forever.

nodes.title: Spanning Tree Algorithm
nodes.summary: The text covers bridge table handling when full, including timeout and replacement options. It introduces the spanning tree algorithm to prevent loops in extended LANs, explaining loop causes, graph theory, root bridge election, designated bridges, and configuration messages. An example illustrates stabilization. It discusses broadcast and multicast forwarding, multicast pruning, and limitations of bridges for connecting similar LANs.

nodes.title: Broadcast and Multicast
nodes.summary: The text explains how bridges handle broadcast and multicast in extended LANs: broadcast forwards frames on all active ports except the source, while multicast can be handled similarly but may be optimized by extending the spanning tree algorithm to prune networks without group members. Bridges learn multicast forwarding by observing source addresses; hosts in a multicast group periodically send frames with the group address as source to a bridge multicast address. This multicast extension is proposed but not widely adopted; today, multicast is implemented like broadcast. The section concludes with bridge limitations, noting they connect only a few similar LANs.

nodes.title: Limitations of Bridges
nodes.summary: This text discusses bridge support for broadcast and multicast, multicast pruning via source observation, and limitations of bridges regarding scale and heterogeneity. It introduces VLANs for scalability, explains VLAN operation with an example, and notes transparency dangers like frame drops, latency variability, and reordering. Finally, it defines internetworks and distinguishes them from the Internet.

This section covers source routing methods (rotation, stripping, pointer) for header handling in datagram and virtual circuit networks, including strict vs. loose source routes. It introduces bridges and LAN switches for interconnecting Ethernets, explaining their operation, differences from repeaters, extended LANs, and bandwidth benefits. It details learning bridges, which inspect source addresses to build forwarding tables with timeouts and flooding, along with implementation structures (BridgeEntry, Map, MAX_TTL). The spanning tree algorithm is introduced to prevent loops, including root bridge election, designated bridges, and configuration messages. Broadcast and multicast handling are discussed, with multicast pruning via source observation. Finally, limitations of bridges regarding scale and heterogeneity are noted, introducing VLANs for scalability and transparency dangers, and defining internetworks versus the Internet.

This section covers switched LANs and bridging, explaining how switches forward packets using headers via datagram, virtual circuit, and source routing approaches. It details datagram forwarding with tables, virtual circuit setup and teardown with VCIs and QoS, and source routing with path specification. It introduces routers for internetworking, discusses switch/router design, and covers bridges and LAN switches, including learning bridges, spanning tree algorithm, VLANs, broadcast/multicast handling, and limitations like scalability and heterogeneity.

nodes.title: 3.2 Basic Internetworking (IP)
3.2.1 What Is an Internetwork?
nodes.summary: The text covers the dangers of transparency in bridged networks, including frame drops, increased latency variability, and potential frame reordering, warning against assuming a single Ethernet. It introduces basic internetworking (IP), defining internetworks as collections of networks providing host-to-host packet delivery, distinguishing lowercase 'internet' from the global Internet. It explains networks, subnetworks, and physical networks, with examples of routers connecting Ethernets, wireless, and point-to-point links. The IP service model is described as best-effort, connectionless datagram delivery with an addressing scheme, emphasizing its simplicity and lack of guarantees, and noting IP's scalability for heterogeneous internetworks.

nodes.title: 3.2.2 Service Model
Datagram Delivery
nodes.summary: The text defines an internetwork's service model, emphasizing host-to-host services over underlying physical networks. It details the IP service model's two parts: addressing and a connectionless, best-effort datagram delivery model. Key aspects include datagram delivery, its unreliable nature, and the benefits of simplicity and flexibility to run over any technology. The text also introduces the IPv4 packet format, covering the header and data structure.

nodes.title: Packet Format
nodes.summary: This text covers IP's design goal of simple routers, its ability to run over any network, and best-effort delivery (packet loss, reordering, duplication). It details the IPv4 packet header fields: Version, HLen, TOS, Length, fragmentation info, TTL, Protocol, Checksum, SourceAddr, DestinationAddr, and options. It then explains fragmentation and reassembly, including MTU, the need for fragmentation, and where it occurs. The text also notes the 32-bit alignment of packet formats and the historical evolution of fields like TOS and TTL.

nodes.title: Fragmentation and Reassembly
nodes.summary: This text covers IP fragmentation and reassembly in internetworking. It explains that networks have different maximum transmission unit (MTU) sizes, necessitating fragmentation when datagrams exceed a network's MTU. Fragmentation occurs at routers, with fragments sharing an identifier for reassembly at the destination host. The process is detailed with header fields like Ident, Flags, and Offset, including an example. Key points: fragments are independent IP datagrams, re-encapsulated per network; reassembly is host-based, not router-based; lost fragments lead to discarded reassembly. The text also introduces global addressing, emphasizing uniqueness and structure for routing, contrasting with Ethernet addresses.

The section defines an internetwork's service model, focusing on host-to-host services. It details the IP service model's addressing and connectionless, best-effort datagram delivery, highlighting unreliability, simplicity, and flexibility. It covers the IPv4 packet format, including header fields and data structure, and design goals like simple routers. Fragmentation and reassembly are explained, covering MTU, fragmentation at routers, reassembly at destinations, and related header fields. Global addressing is introduced, emphasizing uniqueness and structure for routing, contrasting with Ethernet addresses.

nodes.title: 3.2.3 Global Addresses
nodes.summary: The text covers IP fragmentation, including offset calculation using 8-byte chunks, the M bit, and reassembly at the receiving host. It notes fragmentation is undesirable due to lost fragment issues and recommends path MTU discovery. It then explains global addressing: need for uniqueness, Ethernet addresses being flat vs. IP addresses being hierarchical with network and host parts. It describes routers having multiple interfaces, original classful addressing (A, B, C, D, E), bit allocations, host capacities, dotted-decimal notation, and distinction from domain names. Finally, it introduces datagram forwarding basics: destination IP addresses, network part identifying physical networks, and how nodes determine if destinations are on the same network.

nodes.title: 3.2.4 Datagram Forwarding in IP
nodes.summary: The text covers IP datagram forwarding, explaining how routers use network parts of IP addresses and forwarding tables to forward packets. It details the algorithm for direct delivery or next-hop/default router selection, illustrated with examples. It distinguishes bridges, switches, and routers by layering and function. It also discusses hierarchical addressing for scalability, showing how network numbers reduce forwarding table size, and introduces subnetting and classless addressing to address limitations of original IP addressing.

nodes.title: 3.2.5 Subnetting and Classless Addressing
3.2.5 Subnetting and Classless Addressing (intro)
nodes.summary: The text explains how hierarchical IP addressing and subnetting improve scalability by reducing routing table size and information exchange. It covers forwarding tables, ARP, and routing protocols. Subnetting allows one network number to serve multiple physical networks via subnet masks, enabling hosts to determine if destinations are local. Router forwarding tables then use subnet number, mask, and next hop. It also introduces CIDR/supernetting to coalesce classful addresses, addressing inefficient address assignment and excessive router storage, while illustrating aggregation of routing information.

nodes.title: Classless Addressing
nodes.summary: The text introduces Classless Interdomain Routing (CIDR) as an evolution beyond subnetting to address IPv4 inefficiencies and routing scalability. It explains CIDR aggregates classful addresses into supernets using contiguous blocks, illustrated by a 192.4.16/20 example, and introduces slash notation for variable-length prefixes. The text details how CIDR balances efficient address allocation with reduced routing table entries, showing route aggregation across an ISP and its customers via a shared 21-bit prefix. It concludes by noting CIDR's impact on IP forwarding, where prefixes can range from 2 to 32 bits, complicating network number lookups.

nodes.title: IP Forwarding Revisited
nodes.summary: This text covers CIDR route aggregation with an example of eight customers sharing a 21-bit prefix, and the flexibility of variable-length prefixes without requiring equal lengths. It revisits IP forwarding, explaining longest-match routing for overlapping prefixes and referencing the PATRICIA tree algorithm. Finally, it introduces address translation (ARP), describing the need to map IP addresses to link-level addresses like Ethernet, and notes the limitations of encoding physical addresses in IP addresses.

This section on subnetting and classless addressing explains how hierarchical IP addressing and subnetting enhance scalability by reducing routing table size. It covers forwarding tables, ARP, and routing protocols, detailing subnet masks for local destination determination. It introduces CIDR/supernetting to coalesce classful addresses, addressing inefficiencies and routing scalability. CIDR aggregates addresses into supernets using contiguous blocks and slash notation, balancing efficient allocation with reduced routing entries. The section revisits IP forwarding, explaining longest-match routing and the PATRICIA tree algorithm, and introduces address translation (ARP) for mapping IP to link-level addresses, noting limitations of encoding physical addresses in IP addresses.

nodes.title: 3.2.6 Address Translation (ARP)
nodes.summary: The text covers longest-match prefix forwarding, where overlapping prefixes in routing tables are resolved by matching the longest prefix; efficient longest-match algorithms like PATRICIA trees. It details Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) for translating IP addresses to link-level addresses, including dynamic learning via broadcast queries, ARP cache timeouts, and packet format fields. An alternative encoding scheme is mentioned as limited. The text also introduces DHCP for host configuration, explaining that IP addresses must be reconfigurable and include network/host parts, plus default router addresses. Finally, it summarizes IP's mechanisms for heterogeneity and scale through best-effort datagrams, common packet format, global addressing, and hierarchical aggregation.

nodes.title: 3.2.7 Host Configuration (DHCP)
nodes.summary: IP handles heterogeneity via a best-effort model, common packet format with fragmentation/reassembly, and global addressing with ARP; scale via hierarchical network/host addressing. DHCP enables automated host configuration, including server discovery, relay agents, packet format, address leasing, and management trade-offs. ICMP provides error and control messages, including redirects and debugging tools like ping and traceroute. Virtual networks and tunnels are introduced as an increasingly important topic.

nodes.title: 3.2.8 Error Reporting (ICMP)
nodes.summary: The text discusses DHCP's complexity in network management due to dynamic host-IP binding, then covers ICMP for error reporting (e.g., unreachable host, reassembly failure, TTL expiry, checksum failure), control messages like ICMP-Redirect for better routes, and debugging tools ping and traceroute. It concludes by introducing virtual networks and tunnels as an increasingly important IP topic.

nodes.title: 3.2.9 Virtual Networks and Tunnels
nodes.summary: This text covers IP internetworking topics: DHCP's dynamic host-IP binding complicating network management; ICMP error reporting (e.g., unreachable host, TTL expiration) and control messages like redirects, plus debugging tools ping and traceroute; virtual private networks (VPNs) using virtual circuits or IP tunnels, explaining tunnel encapsulation, forwarding tables, benefits (security, multicast, non-IP protocols, forced delivery), and drawbacks (overhead, fragmentation, management); and the distinction between forwarding (per-packet table lookup) and routing (building forwarding tables via distributed algorithms).

Section 3.2 covers IP internetworking, starting with internetwork concepts and the best-effort, connectionless IP service model. It details IPv4 packet format, fragmentation and reassembly, and global hierarchical addressing. Datagram forwarding, subnetting, and classless addressing (CIDR) are explained, including longest-match routing. Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) maps IP to link-level addresses. Host configuration via DHCP and error reporting through ICMP (with ping/traceroute) are described. Finally, virtual networks and tunnels, including VPNs, are introduced, distinguishing forwarding from routing.

nodes.title: 3.3 Routing
3.3 Routing (intro)
nodes.summary: The text first notes the management cost of tunnels. It then introduces routing, distinguishing it from forwarding: forwarding is local packet handling, while routing builds forwarding tables via distributed algorithms. It differentiates forwarding and routing tables, with examples. It states that intradomain routing protocols (IGPs) suit small to midsized networks, not the Internet-scale. Routing is framed as a graph theory problem, with nodes and edges with costs, aiming to find the lowest-cost path.

nodes.title: 3.3.1 Network as a Graph
nodes.summary: This text defines intradomain routing protocols (IGPs) for networks under single administrative control, focusing on small to midsized networks. It introduces routing as a graph theory problem, where nodes represent routers and edges represent links with associated costs. The goal is finding the lowest-cost path. Static routing's shortcomings (failure handling, changes, scalability) lead to distributed, dynamic routing protocols. Challenges of distributed algorithms, like routing loops, are noted. The text previews distance-vector and link-state protocols and mentions RIP, with edge cost calculation deferred to Section 3.3.4.

nodes.title: 3.3.2 Distance-Vector (RIP)
3.3.2 Distance-Vector (RIP) (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers routing protocols, focusing on distance-vector routing and RIP. It contrasts static routing's shortcomings with dynamic, distributed protocols. It explains distance-vector operation, including initial distance tables, neighbor updates, convergence, and the count-to-infinity problem with solutions like split horizon and poison reverse. It details update mechanisms (periodic and triggered), failure detection, and link failure effects. Implementation aspects are shown via code structures (Route, MAX_TTL) and the mergeRoute routine, including TTL management.

nodes.title: Implementation
nodes.summary: The text details routing algorithm implementation with structures (Route, MAX_TTL), functions (mergeRoute, updateRoutingTable), and TTL handling. It introduces RIP as a distance-vector protocol, explaining router advertisements of network costs and the RIP v2 packet format with address, mask, distance triples. RIP sends updates every 30 seconds and updates routes based on lower cost.

nodes.title: Routing Information Protocol (RIP)
nodes.summary: The text covers Routing Information Protocol (RIP), a widely used distance-vector routing protocol distributed with BSD Unix. It explains that routers advertise costs to reach networks rather than routers, as shown in an example network and the RIPv2 packet format containing address, mask, and distance triples. RIP sends updates every 30 seconds or when routing tables change, supports multiple address families, and RIPv2 introduced subnet masks. RIP uses hop count as its metric, with valid distances 1-15 and 16 as infinity, limiting it to small networks. The text also introduces link-state routing (OSPF) as the second major intradomain routing protocol.

This section covers distance-vector routing and RIP, contrasting static and dynamic protocols. It explains distance-vector operation: initial tables, neighbor updates, convergence, and the count-to-infinity problem with solutions like split horizon and poison reverse. It details update mechanisms (periodic and triggered), failure detection, and link failure effects. Implementation aspects are shown via code structures (Route, MAX_TTL) and the mergeRoute routine, including TTL management. RIP is introduced as a widely used distance-vector protocol distributed with BSD Unix, advertising costs to networks. The RIPv2 packet format with address, mask, and distance triples is explained. RIP sends updates every 30 seconds or when tables change, supports multiple address families, and uses hop count as its metric (valid 1-15, 16 as infinity), limiting it to small networks. Link-state routing (OSPF) is introduced as the second major intradomain routing protocol.

nodes.title: 3.3.3 Link State (OSPF)
3.3.3 Link State (OSPF) (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers RIPv2 packet format and features, including support for multiple address families, subnet masks, equal link costs of 1, distance limits of 15 hops, and the use of infinity as 16. It also discusses link-state routing (OSPF), explaining that each node knows its neighbors' states and costs, and that link-state information is disseminated to build a complete network map. Reliable flooding is described, involving link-state packets with node ID, neighbor list, sequence number, and TTL, and the challenges of achieving reliable flooding.

nodes.title: Reliable Flooding
nodes.summary: Link-state routing relies on reliable flooding of link-state packets (LSPs) and route calculation. Reliable flooding ensures all nodes receive LSPs, which contain node ID, neighbors with link costs, sequence number, and TTL. Flooding uses acknowledgments, sequence numbers, and TTL to manage reliability, avoid old information, and reduce overhead. LSPs are generated periodically or on topology changes, detected via link-layer or hello packets. Route calculation uses Dijkstra's algorithm, specifically the forward search algorithm, to compute shortest paths from accumulated LSPs.

nodes.title: Route Calculation
nodes.summary: The text explains route calculation in link-state routing using Dijkstra's algorithm, including graph-theoretic definitions, algorithm steps, and the forward search algorithm with Tentative and Confirmed lists, illustrated with an example network and routing table. It discusses link-state algorithm properties like quick stabilization and low traffic, versus drawbacks like large storage, and contrasts it with distance-vector. It introduces OSPF as a link-state protocol, covering features such as authentication, hierarchy, and load balancing, and describes OSPF message header fields.

nodes.title: The Open Shortest Path First Protocol (OSPF)
nodes.summary: OSPF, a widely used open link-state routing protocol created by IETF, adds authentication, hierarchical areas, and load balancing to basic link-state routing. It details OSPF message types, header format, and link-state advertisements (LSAs), including fields like LS Age, sequence number, checksum, and link-state information with TOS support. It also discusses routing metrics, covering simple hop counts, drawbacks like ignoring latency, capacity, and load, and ARPANET's role in testing link-cost calculation and demonstrating link-state routing's stability.

The section covers RIPv2 packet format and features, including multiple address families, subnet masks, equal link costs of 1, distance limits of 15 hops, and infinity as 16. It introduces link-state routing (OSPF), where each node knows its neighbors' states and costs, and link-state information is disseminated to build a complete network map. Reliable flooding is described, involving link-state packets with node ID, neighbor list, sequence number, and TTL, and the challenges of achieving reliable flooding. It details reliable flooding mechanisms, route calculation using Dijkstra's algorithm with forward search, Tentative and Confirmed lists, and an example. It contrasts link-state with distance-vector, and introduces OSPF, covering authentication, hierarchy, load balancing, message types, header format, LSAs, routing metrics, and ARPANET's role in testing link-cost calculation.

nodes.title: 3.3.4 Metrics
nodes.summary: This text from a networking chapter covers OSPF link-state details, including Link ID, Link Data, metrics, and TOS-based routing (noting limited deployment). It then discusses routing metrics: simple hop count drawbacks, ARPANET's evolution from queue length to delay-based metrics, instability issues, and the revised metric with smoothing and compressed dynamic range. It notes static metrics are now common. Monitoring routing behavior is examined via Paxson's traceroute study on route failures, stability, and asymmetry. Finally, it introduces implementation and performance of switches and routers using general-purpose processors.

Section 3.3 covers routing, starting with tunnel management costs and distinguishing forwarding from routing. It frames routing as a graph theory problem, then details intradomain routing protocols (IGPs) for small to midsized networks. It explains distance-vector routing with RIP, including operation, count-to-infinity problem, solutions like split horizon, update mechanisms, and RIPv2 packet format. It also covers link-state routing with OSPF, including reliable flooding, Dijkstra's algorithm, and contrasts with distance-vector. Finally, it discusses routing metrics, ARPANET's evolution to delay-based metrics, monitoring via traceroute, and switch/router implementation.

nodes.title: 3.4 Implementation and performance
3.4 Implementation and performance (intro)
nodes.summary: The text discusses monitoring Internet routing behavior, noting complexity and fault diagnosis challenges, and citing Paxson's traceroute study on route failures, stability, symmetry, and unpredictability. It then introduces implementation and performance, describing a general-purpose processor with network interfaces and DMA as a simple switch or router design, and begins switch basics, using 'switch' to cover routers due to similar internal designs.

nodes.title: 3.4.1 Switch Basics
nodes.summary: This section covers switch and router implementation, focusing on performance. It explains using general-purpose processors as switches via DMA, noting throughput limits from shared bus/memory contention and packet processing overhead, especially for short packets. It discusses switch design goals to reduce contention and increase parallel throughput. The difficulty of defining throughput is addressed, considering traffic patterns, packet sizes, and the need for both bit-per-second and packet-per-second rates. Traffic modeling challenges are mentioned. Finally, it describes switch architecture with input/output ports, a switch fabric, and a control processor.

nodes.title: 3.4.2 Ports
nodes.summary: The text discusses challenges in modeling computer networks due to rapid evolution, contrasting with stable telephone traffic. It covers switch architecture, including ports, fabrics, and control processors, with a diagram of a 4x4 switch. Performance bottlenecks in input ports and head-of-line blocking are explained. Buffering functions and quality of service are addressed. Fabric types—shared bus, shared memory, and crossbar—are described, emphasizing parallelism and throughput.

nodes.title: 3.4.3 Fabrics
nodes.summary: This text covers switch and router implementation. It explains buffer management for QoS, then describes switch fabrics: shared bus, shared memory, crossbar, and self-routing (including banyan networks, collisions, and Batcher-banyan design). It notes various switch types using these fabrics. Router implementation follows, covering control processor, switch fabric, ports, handling variable-length packets via segmentation and reassembly (SAR), cell-based fabrics, and performance characterization challenges compared to ATM switches.

nodes.title: 3.4.4 Router Implementation
nodes.summary: Router implementation: like switches, routers use control processors, switching fabrics, and ports. Key differences: handling variable-length packets, requiring segmentation and re-assembly, and performance characterization based on packet size. Forwarding models are centralized or distributed. IP forwarding complexity involves variable-length lookups. Advances enable high-speed routers and network processors, which are debated versus ASICs. The chapter summary covers LAN switches, IP for heterogeneity, ARP, routing algorithms (RIP, OSPF), and switch/router scaling with contention and specialized hardware.

Section 3.4 covers switch and router implementation and performance. It begins with monitoring routing behavior and fault diagnosis, citing Paxson's traceroute study, then introduces basic switch design using general-purpose processors with DMA, discussing throughput limits, contention, and design goals. Subsections detail switch basics, including traffic modeling and architecture; ports, covering head-of-line blocking, buffering, QoS, and fabrics; fabrics, describing shared bus, shared memory, crossbar, and self-routing (banyan, Batcher-banyan); and router implementation, focusing on variable-length packet handling, segmentation and reassembly, forwarding models, IP lookups, and network processors versus ASICs. The section concludes with a chapter summary on LAN switches, IP, ARP, routing algorithms, and scaling.

nodes.title: 3.5 Summary
nodes.summary: The text summarizes internetworking concepts: LAN switches/bridges use source address learning and spanning tree algorithms; IP enables heterogeneous networks with best-effort datagrams and global addressing, using ARP for address translation. Routing algorithms include link-state and distance-vector (RIP, OSPF). Switches and routers need high performance and scalability, often using special-purpose hardware due to contention. The Internet's success is noted, and the 'Future Internet' section discusses clean-slate research, including mobility-based identifiers and new trust models for security.

nodes.title: What’s Next: The Future Internet
nodes.summary: This text discusses the Internet's success, the question of what comes after it, and 'Future Internet' research, including clean-slate approaches. It provides examples like mobility and trust models, and notes that the Internet will continue to evolve. It also includes a 'Further Reading' section listing seminal papers on bridges, TCP/IP, switch design, ATM, and RFCs for subnetting, CIDR, RIPv2, and OSPF.

nodes.title: Further Reading
nodes.summary: The text discusses the Internet's evolving architecture and Incrementally deployable research, then lists further reading, including seminal papers on bridges (Perlman), TCP/IP (Cerf and Kahn), and switch design (McKeown). It cites RFCs for subnetting, CIDR, RIPv2, and OSPF, notes IP fragmentation and Path MTU discovery, and references future Internet research (Clark et al.) and live NSF/GENI links. It also covers switch architectures, Batcher networks, sorting networks, crossbar switches, the Sunshine switch, fast IP lookup algorithms, optical networking, queuing theory, traffic modeling, and long-range dependence. Finally, it presents exercises on virtual circuit tables using a given network diagram.

nodes.title: Exercises
nodes.summary: This chapter excerpt on internetworking provides live references for Future Internet Design and GENI, then presents 75 exercises covering virtual circuit and datagram forwarding tables, source routing, spanning tree algorithm, learning bridges, ATM cell switching, switch performance, banyan and Batcher networks, IP addressing, fragmentation, ARP, distance-vector and link-state routing, CIDR, and subnetting. It concludes with an introduction to advanced internetworking, emphasizing scaling challenges and hierarchical routing with BGP.

summary: Chapter 3 on Internetworking covers interconnecting heterogeneous networks via switches, bridges, and routers. It details packet forwarding methods (datagram, virtual circuit, source routing), IP service model, IPv4 addressing, subnetting, CIDR, ARP, DHCP, ICMP, and tunnels. Routing algorithms include distance-vector (RIP) and link-state (OSPF), with metrics and implementation. Switch/router design and performance are addressed, including architectures, contention, and fabrics. The chapter concludes with a summary, future internet research, further reading, and 75 exercises on related topics.

title: Chapter 4. Advanced Internetworking

nodes.title: Problem: Scaling to Billions
nodes.summary: The text addresses advanced internetworking challenges: heterogeneity and scale. It discusses the Internet's rapid growth, the need for hierarchical routing to handle billions of nodes, and BGP for interdomain routing. It covers IPv6's expanded addressing and features. It introduces enhancements like multicast for group delivery, MPLS for modified forwarding, and mobility support for mobile hosts/routers. It notes scalability concerns for each. The chapter then introduces the global Internet's structure, emphasizing its organizational shape and the inadequacy of traditional routing protocols for hundreds of thousands of networks.

nodes.title: 4.1 The Global Internet
4.1 The Global Internet (intro)
nodes.summary: This text covers advanced internetworking, starting with IPv6's expanded address space and features. It discusses scalability challenges in routing and addressing, and introduces enhancements like multicast, MPLS, and mobility support. It then examines the global Internet's structure in 1990, including end-user sites, regional networks, and the NSFNET backbone, highlighting administrative independence and autonomous systems. The text details two scaling issues: routing scalability and address utilization, emphasizing hierarchy. It describes routing areas in link-state protocols like OSPF, including backbone area and area border routers, to improve scalability within domains.

nodes.title: 4.1.1 Routing Areas
nodes.summary: The text discusses scalability challenges in the Internet, focusing on routing scalability and address utilization. It highlights hierarchy and aggregation as key principles, exemplified by CIDR and subnetting. It details routing areas in link-state protocols like OSPF, including area types, area border routers, and the trade-off between scalability and optimal routing. It introduces virtual links for backbone flexibility. Finally, it covers interdomain routing with BGP, explaining autonomous systems and the division into intradomain and interdomain routing for improved scalability.

nodes.title: 4.1.2 Interdomain Routing (BGP)
4.1.2 Interdomain Routing (BGP) (intro)
nodes.summary: This text covers interdomain routing using BGP. It defines autonomous systems (AS) as networks under single administrative control, e.g., ISPs, and explains their role in hierarchical routing aggregation for scalability. The routing problem is split into intradomain and interdomain routing. Interdomain routing involves sharing reachability information between ASs, each running its own intradomain protocols. Key challenges include supporting complex routing policies, such as preferring one AS over another and avoiding transit traffic, while keeping policies private and independent. The text notes two major interdomain protocols, starting with EGP and its limitations.

nodes.title: Challenges in Interdomain Routing
nodes.summary: The text covers interdomain routing, starting with the autonomous system (AS) model that decouples intradomain and interdomain routing. It discusses challenges like routing policies, transit traffic, and the need for private, policy-compliant, loop-free paths. It contrasts the limited Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) with the more flexible Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), and describes AS types (stub, multihomed, transit). Key issues include scalability, lack of meaningful path costs, and trust. The basics of BGP are introduced, including border routers and BGP speakers.

nodes.title: Basics of BGP
nodes.summary: The text covers interdomain routing challenges including 300,000 prefixes, autonomous systems' unique metrics, reachability-only advertisements, and trust issues. It details BGP as a path-vector protocol advertising complete AS paths to enable policies and detect loops, with examples of loop prevention using unique AS numbers. BGP UPDATE messages carry positive and negative (withdrawn) reachability, run over TCP with keepalives, and allow policies like no transit. Border routers, BGP speakers, and 16-bit AS numbers (now 32-bit) are explained.

nodes.title: Common AS Relationships and Policies
nodes.summary: This text discusses BGP routing policies and hierarchical Internet structure, including stub networks, providers, peers, and Tier-1 providers, and how this hierarchy aids scalability. It then explains integrating interdomain and intradomain routing: using default routes in stub ASes, injecting specific external routes, and using iBGP in backbone networks to distribute BGP information without overburdening intradomain protocols. An example network illustrates how routers combine iBGP and IGP data to build complete forwarding tables. Finally, it introduces IPv6 as a response to IP address exhaustion, noting CIDR's role in delaying exhaustion and controlling routing table growth.

nodes.title: 4.1.3 IP Version 6 (IPv6)
4.1.3 IP Version 6 (IPv6) (intro)
nodes.summary: The text explains interdomain and intradomain routing using BGP, showing how routers combine iBGP, eBGP, and IGP information to build complete routing tables, as illustrated in Figures 4.9 and 4.10. It then introduces IPv6, motivated by IP address exhaustion despite CIDR, noting the need for a larger address space due to increasing device connectivity. It briefly covers the IETF's 1991 efforts to expand the address space, the challenges of changing the IP header, and the need for new software across the Internet.

nodes.title: Historical Perspective
nodes.summary: The text covers Section 4.1 on the global internet, presenting a figure with BGP, IGP, and combined routing tables at router B. It discusses IPv4 address exhaustion due to inefficient utilization and new device types. It details the historical development of IPv6, starting with IETF's 1991 IPng effort, the wish list features (real-time services, security, autoconfiguration, enhanced routing), and the transition plan. It describes the IPng Directorate's selection of SIPP, leading to a 128-bit address space. Finally, it explains IPv6 addressing and routing, including the 128-bit space, address efficiency estimates, and classless address space allocation with leading bits denoting different uses.

nodes.title: Addresses and Routing
nodes.summary: The text details the selection of SIPP as the basis for IPng, leading to IPv6 with a 128-bit address space after initial 64-bit proposal. It covers IPv6's vast address capacity compared to IPv4, empirical efficiency estimates, classless address space allocation using leading bits for different uses, and the dominance of Global Unicast Addresses, including CIDR influence and prefix assignments.

nodes.title: Address Space Allocation
nodes.summary: The text discusses IPv6's development from SIPP, its 128-bit address space, and enhanced capacity versus IPv4. It covers address space allocation using classless prefixes for multicast, link-local, site-local, and global unicast addresses, including IPv4-compatible and mapped addresses. It also outlines address notation with hexadecimal colon-separated segments.

nodes.title: Address Notation
nodes.summary: Table 4.1 outlines IPv6 address prefix assignments: unspecified, loopback, multicast, link-local unicast, and global unicast. It explains special IPv4-compatible and IPv4-mapped addresses, then details IPv6 address notation including hexadecimal format, zero compression with double colon, and embedded IPv4 notation. The transition from IPv4 to IPv6 is discussed, emphasizing incremental deployment via dual-stack operation and tunneling, with automatic tunneling using IPv4-mapped addresses or manual configuration. Finally, global unicast address allocation is described, comparing it to CIDR and defining hierarchy terms like subscriber, provider, direct, and indirect providers.

nodes.title: Global Unicast Addresses
nodes.summary: IPv6 shorthand notation for contiguous zeros and embedded IPv4 addresses. Global unicast address allocation uses provider-based hierarchy similar to CIDR for scalable routing aggregation, with terms like subscriber, provider, direct, indirect, and backbone networks. Discusses benefits, drawbacks of renumbering, geographic addressing, and aggregation at continental levels. Address assignment advantages over IPv4. Multi-provider subscriber issues. Packet format: simpler header, Version, TrafficClass, FlowLabel, PayloadLen, and NextHeader fields.

nodes.title: Packet Format
Packet Format (intro)
nodes.summary: This text covers IPv6 provider-based unicast addresses, including address assignment and multi-provider subscriber challenges with prefix solutions. It details the simplified IPv6 packet header format, comparing it to IPv4, and explains fields like Version, TrafficClass, FlowLabel, PayloadLen, NextHeader, and HopLimit. It discusses IPv6 extension headers for options and fragmentation, emphasizing efficiency over IPv4. Autoconfiguration is addressed, including stateless autoconfiguration for interface IDs and subnet prefixes without a server. Finally, it introduces Network Address Translation (NAT) as a method to conserve IP address space using private addresses.

nodes.title: Autoconfiguration
nodes.summary: The text discusses IPv6's NextHeader field with an authentication header example. It covers autoconfiguration, noting that Internet growth was hindered by required system administration expertise for configuring IP addresses, subnet masks, and name servers. IPv6's goal is plug-and-play operation, using stateless autoconfiguration without a server, dividing into obtaining a unique interface ID and correct address prefix. It also introduces Network Address Translation (NAT) as a popular method to conserve IP address space, using private addresses, and notes its role in delaying IPv6 deployment despite being considered architecturally impure.

nodes.title: Network Address Translation
nodes.summary: The text covers IPv6 autoconfiguration (stateless and DHCP-based), including interface ID and prefix acquisition, and the role of 128-bit addresses. It details Network Address Translation (NAT): private addresses, NAT box translation, drawbacks like breaking global uniqueness and complicating higher-layer protocols and inbound connections, and reasons for NAT's persistence. It also describes IPv6 advanced routing via the routing header, including provider selection and anycast addresses for targeting topological areas.

nodes.title: Advanced Routing Capabilities
nodes.summary: This section discusses IPv6 addressing and routing. It explains forming link-local addresses from unique 48-bit link-level addresses (e.g., Ethernet) using a specific prefix, which suffices for isolated devices, while globally valid addresses require router-advertised prefixes with space for link-level addresses. Embedding 48-bit addresses motivated IPv6's 128-bit size, also allowing hierarchical addressing. It introduces advanced routing via the routing header, which lists IPv6 addresses for nodes or topological areas to visit, enabling provider selection for cost, reliability, or security. Anycast addresses, assigned to interface sets, route packets to the nearest interface, used in routing headers.

The Packet Format section covers IPv6 provider-based unicast address assignment, multi-provider subscriber issues, and the simplified packet header fields (Version, TrafficClass, FlowLabel, PayloadLen, NextHeader, HopLimit) compared to IPv4, plus extension headers for options and fragmentation. It details stateless and DHCP-based autoconfiguration for interface IDs and prefixes, addressing plug-and-play goals. Network Address Translation (NAT) is explained for conserving IP space via private addresses, including translation, drawbacks (breaking global uniqueness, complicating protocols), and persistence. Advanced routing capabilities include the routing header for provider selection and anycast addresses, as well as link-local address formation from 48-bit link-level addresses and the rationale for IPv6's 128-bit size.

nodes.title: Advanced Routing Capabilities
nodes.summary: IPv6 link-local addresses derive from unique link-level addresses (e.g., 48-bit Ethernet) with a prefix and zero padding, needing routers for global prefixes. Embedding 48-bit addresses motivated 128-bit size for multilevel hierarchy. The routing header lists IPv6 addresses for topological areas, enabling provider selection per packet (e.g., cheap, reliable, secure). Anycast addresses target nearest interface in a set, aiding backbone routers and mobile hosts. Other IPv6 features include autoconfiguration, source-directed routing, mobility, security, and a new service model. IPv4 and IPv6 capabilities converge, but larger addresses drive IPv6. Multicast supports one-to-many (radio, news) and many-to-many (teleconferencing, gaming) applications, unlike unicast IP which wastes bandwidth.

nodes.title: Other Features
nodes.summary: The text covers IPv6's anycast address and routing header for enhanced mobile host routing, with mechanisms still being defined. It discusses IPv6's other features: autoconfiguration, source-directed routing, mobility, network security, and a new service model, noting IPv4 and IPv6 capabilities are virtually indistinguishable, with larger addresses as the main IPv6 driver. It then introduces multicast: hardware multicast in multi-access networks like Ethernet, but broader internetwork multicasting for one-to-many (radio, news, stock prices, software updates) and many-to-many (teleconferencing, gaming, distributed simulations) applications. Normal IP unicast is inefficient for groups, causing redundant bandwidth consumption.

This section covers IPv6, motivated by IPv4 address exhaustion. It traces IPv6's historical development from the IETF's 1991 IPng effort to the selection of SIPP with a 128-bit address space. It details address allocation, notation, global unicast addresses, and the simplified packet format. Transition mechanisms like dual-stack and tunneling are explained. Advanced features include routing headers, anycast, autoconfiguration, and security. The section also introduces multicast for one-to-many and many-to-many applications, contrasting it with inefficient unicast.

This section covers interdomain routing with BGP, defining autonomous systems (AS) and their role in hierarchical routing aggregation. It contrasts intradomain and interdomain routing, highlighting challenges like routing policies, transit traffic, privacy, loop-free paths, scalability, and trust. It compares EGP and BGP, describes AS types (stub, multihomed, transit), and introduces BGP basics: path-vector protocol, AS paths, UPDATE messages over TCP, border routers, BGP speakers, and 16/32-bit AS numbers. It discusses common AS relationships (stub, provider, peer, Tier-1), integrating interdomain and intradomain routing using default routes, iBGP, and IGPs. Finally, it introduces IPv6: motivation, history, 128-bit addressing, notation, simplified packet format, transition mechanisms (dual-stack, tunneling), advanced features (routing headers, anycast, autoconfiguration, security), and multicast.

This section covers advanced internetworking, focusing on IPv6's expanded addressing and features, and scalability challenges in routing and addressing. It examines the global Internet's historical structure, including autonomous systems, and details hierarchical solutions like routing areas in OSPF and CIDR. Interdomain routing with BGP is explained, covering autonomous system types, path-vector protocol, AS relationships, and integration with intradomain routing. IPv6 is introduced with its motivation, addressing, transition mechanisms, and advanced features like multicast and security.

nodes.title: 4.2 Multicast
4.2 Multicast (intro)
nodes.summary: The text discusses IPv6's anycast address and routing header for enhanced mobile routing, plus other IPv6 features like autoconfiguration and source-directed routing, noting IPv4 and IPv6 capabilities are converging. It then introduces IP multicast for one-to-many and many-to-many communication, contrasting it with unicast. It describes the basic many-to-many multicast model, Source-Specific Multicast (SSM), and Any Source Multicast (ASM). It covers host group management via IGMP (IPv4) and MLD (IPv6), and multicast address allocation, including IPv4 class D and IPv6 ranges, and the mapping of IP multicast addresses to Ethernet multicast addresses.

nodes.title: 4.2.1 Multicast Addresses
4.2.1 Multicast Addresses (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers advanced internetworking multicast topics: Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) vs Any Source Multicast (ASM); host group management via IGMP (IPv4) and MLD (IPv6), including router polling; multicast address ranges in IPv4 (class D) and IPv6, and the challenge of mapping 28-bit IPv4 multicast addresses to 23-bit Ethernet multicast addresses, causing unintended traffic and host filtering; mitigation in switched networks; out-of-band group address advertisement (e.g., sdr); multicast routing concepts like distribution trees and forwarding tables based on address and source; and introduces DVMRP for multicast routing.

nodes.title: 4.2.2 Multicast Routing (DVMRP, PIM, MSDP)
nodes.summary: This section covers multicast addressing issues, including mismatches and mitigation, and how senders and receivers learn addresses. It introduces multicast routing, detailing forwarding tables and distribution trees. It describes DVMRP's flood-and-prune approach using Reverse Path Broadcast, parent routers, and pruning, noting its overhead. It then covers PIM, contrasting dense and sparse modes, with PIM-SM using rendezvous points, Join messages, shared and source-specific trees, and protocol independence.

nodes.title: PIM-SM
nodes.summary: PIM-SM, a scalable multicast protocol, uses explicit Join messages and a rendezvous point (RP) to build shared trees, later optimized with source-specific trees. It is unicast-protocol-independent. It tunnels packets to the RP, then establishes source-specific state. Interdomain multicast issues arise because a single RP conflicts with domain autonomy, so PIM-SM is typically used only within a domain.

nodes.title: Interdomain Multicast (MSDP)
nodes.summary: This text covers PIM-SM's source-specific tree creation, where routers send joins toward the source, building (S, G) state and bypassing the RP, while the shared tree is retained for new senders. It explains PIM's unicast routing protocol independence, then addresses interdomain multicast via MSDP, which links RPs across domains using TCP and broadcasts source-active messages through Reverse Path Broadcast. MSDP enables RPs with receivers to join source-specific trees. Finally, it introduces PIM-SSM for one-to-many applications, extending PIM-SM's source-specific optimization to a service model where only one sender is legitimate.

nodes.title: Source-Specific Multicast (PIM-SSM)
nodes.summary: The text covers extending multicast across domains using MSDP to connect PIM-SM domains' RPs via TCP, forming a mesh that broadcasts Source Active messages and enabling source-specific joins. It then describes PIM-SSM, a one-to-many model using channels (source S, group G), specified in IGMP Membership Reports, bypassing shared trees for direct source-specific trees, with benefits like direct paths, address reuse, reduced attack risk, and cross-domain use without MSDP. Finally, it introduces BIDIR-PIM for many-to-many multicasting, using bidirectional shared trees rooted at an RP, allowing packets to flow up and down branches, with no actual RP needed, only a routable address.

nodes.title: Bidirectional Trees (BIDIR-PIM)
nodes.summary: The text covers multicast protocols, focusing on PIM-SSM and BIDIR-PIM. PIM-SSM benefits include direct multicast travel, independent address use across domains, reduced attack risk, and cross-domain operation without MSDP. BIDIR-PIM suits many-to-many multicasting, using a bidirectional shared tree rooted at a routable RP address, eliminating source registration and reducing state and bottleneck issues. It also discusses the fate of multicast protocols like DVMRP, MOSPF, PIM-DM, CBT, and BGMP, noting scaling challenges and limited adoption. The text concludes that multicast is a complex space requiring optimization choices. Finally, it introduces MPLS, combining virtual circuit and datagram properties for IP capabilities on non-IP devices.

This section covers multicast addressing, including Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) versus Any Source Multicast (ASM), host group management via IGMP and MLD, IPv4 and IPv6 multicast address ranges, and mapping issues between IPv4 and Ethernet addresses with mitigation strategies. It also details multicast routing protocols: DVMRP's flood-and-prune approach, PIM (dense and sparse modes), PIM-SM with rendezvous points and shared/source-specific trees, interdomain multicast via MSDP, PIM-SSM for one-to-many applications, and BIDIR-PIM for many-to-many. It discusses the fate of various multicast protocols and introduces MPLS for combining virtual circuit and datagram properties.

The section covers IPv6 anycast, routing, and convergence with IPv4, then introduces IP multicast models: many-to-many, SSM, and ASM. It details host group management via IGMP and MLD, multicast address allocation for IPv4 and IPv6, and Ethernet mapping. It explains multicast routing protocols: DVMRP, PIM (dense and sparse modes), PIM-SM with rendezvous points, interdomain multicast via MSDP, PIM-SSM, BIDIR-PIM, and MPLS for combining virtual circuit and datagram properties.

nodes.title: 4.3 Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS)
4.3 Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) (intro)
nodes.summary: The text discusses advantages of bidirectional multicast trees over PIM-SM, noting more direct routes, less state, and no RP bottleneck, while acknowledging longer paths. It concludes multicast optimization requires trade-offs based on criteria like bandwidth and application type. It then introduces MPLS as combining virtual circuits and datagrams, using IP routing with short labels. Three main current uses are listed: enabling IP on non-IP devices, forwarding along explicit routes, and supporting VPNs, with performance improvement no longer a goal. The chapter begins explaining destination-based forwarding with an example network.

nodes.title: 4.3.1 Destination-Based Forwarding
4.3.1 Destination-Based Forwarding (intro)
nodes.summary: This text covers MPLS, including its goals: forwarding IP packets along explicit routes and supporting VPN services, but not improving performance. It explains destination-based forwarding with an example: routers allocate labels per prefix, advertise them via Label Distribution Protocol, and forward packets using label swapping (exact match) instead of longest-match IP lookup. Labels are attached as shim headers between Layer 2 and 3 or in ATM cell headers, enabling devices like ATM and optical switches to become Label Switching Routers. It introduces the concept of Forwarding Equivalence Classes (FECs) and discusses MPLS's place in layered architectures, often called a layer 2.5 protocol.

nodes.title: What Layer is MPLS?
nodes.summary: The text explains MPLS label placement: a "shim" between layer 2 and 3 headers for frame-based links, or in ATM cell headers for ATM switches acting as LSRs. It debates MPLS's layer (often 2.5) due to its position and use of IP protocols. Benefits of MPLS over overlay ATM networks include fewer routing adjacencies, full topology view for edge routers, and software-only upgrades, plus "ships in the night" mode and GMPLS extension to optical/STDM devices. It also covers explicit routing, contrasting it with source routing, and illustrates traffic engineering with a fish network example.

nodes.title: 4.3.2 Explicit Routing
nodes.summary: Section 4.3.2 on explicit routing in MPLS discusses source routing's limitations in IP, explains MPLS explicit routing where routers (not the source) choose paths, and illustrates with a fish network (R1-R7 tail, R7 head). It gives examples of directing traffic from R1 to R7 via R1-R3-R6-R7 and from R2 to R7 via R2-R3-R4-R5-R7 to use capacity, forming two forwarding equivalence classes. Normal IP struggles because R3 ignores origin, but MPLS label swapping enables the desired paths if routers are MPLS-enabled.

This section covers MPLS destination-based forwarding, including its goals (forwarding IP packets along explicit routes, supporting VPNs) and label-swapping mechanism with per-prefix labels, Label Distribution Protocol, and shim headers between layers 2 and 3 or in ATM cells. It introduces Forwarding Equivalence Classes and debates MPLS's layer (often 2.5). Benefits over overlay ATM include fewer adjacencies, full topology view, software-only upgrades, 'ships in the night' mode, and GMPLS extension. Explicit routing is explained: routers (not source) choose paths, illustrated with a fish network and two FECs, contrasting with normal IP limitations and showing label swapping enables desired paths.

nodes.title: 4.3.2 Explicit Routing
nodes.summary: This section covers MPLS explicit routing, including source routing limitations, a fish network example requiring specific paths for different FECs, and the use of RSVP to set up label forwarding along explicit paths. It discusses applications like traffic engineering and fast reroute, plus automatic route calculation with CSPF. It then introduces MPLS for VPNs and tunnels, focusing on layer 2 VPNs and pseudowire emulation (e.g., ATM circuits), explaining how IP tunnels encapsulate and forward non-IP data.

nodes.title: 4.3.3 Virtual Private Networks and Tunnels
4.3.3 Virtual Private Networks and Tunnels (intro)
nodes.summary: The text discusses MPLS for building VPNs and tunnels, focusing on layer 2 VPNs and pseudowire emulation. It explains how MPLS tunnels encapsulate layer 2 data like ATM cells, contrasting with IP tunnels, and details the use of stacked MPLS labels for forwarding and demultiplexing. A step-by-step example illustrates ATM circuit emulation, including configuration of head and tail routers and packet forwarding with dual labels. It notes MPLS benefits such as shorter headers and scalability, mentions application to other layer 2 services like Frame Relay and Ethernet, and briefly covers layer 3 VPNs.

nodes.title: 6. ATM cells sent 202
nodes.summary: This text covers MPLS applications and mobile networking challenges. It details MPLS label stacking and tunneling for layer 2 services (e.g., ATM, Frame Relay, Ethernet) and layer 3 VPNs, where service providers create isolated private IP networks. The text also discusses MPLS deployment, notably for layer 3 VPNs and explicit routing for traffic engineering. Finally, it introduces challenges for mobile devices, such as obtaining new IP addresses when moving between networks and the need for mechanisms to maintain connections during handoffs.

The section covers MPLS for building VPNs and tunnels, focusing on layer 2 VPNs and pseudowire emulation. It explains MPLS tunnels encapsulating layer 2 data like ATM cells, contrasting with IP tunnels, and details stacked MPLS labels for forwarding and demultiplexing. A step-by-step ATM circuit emulation example includes head and tail router configuration and packet forwarding with dual labels. It notes MPLS benefits like shorter headers and scalability, application to Frame Relay and Ethernet, and briefly covers layer 3 VPNs. It also discusses MPLS deployment for layer 3 VPNs and traffic engineering, and mobile networking challenges like obtaining new IP addresses and maintaining connections during handoffs.

Section 4.3 introduces MPLS as a technology combining virtual circuits and datagrams, using IP routing with short labels. It lists main uses: enabling IP on non-IP devices, forwarding along explicit routes, and supporting VPNs. Subsection 4.3.1 covers destination-based forwarding, label-swapping, Label Distribution Protocol, shim headers, Forwarding Equivalence Classes, and benefits over overlay ATM. Subsection 4.3.2 explains explicit routing, source routing limitations, RSVP for label forwarding, traffic engineering, fast reroute, and CSPF. Subsection 4.3.3 details MPLS for VPNs and tunnels, including layer 2 VPNs, pseudowire emulation, stacked labels, ATM circuit emulation example, benefits, layer 3 VPNs, deployment, and mobile networking challenges.

nodes.title: 4.4 Routing Amoung Mobile Devices
4.4.1 Challenges for Mobile Networking
nodes.summary: This section discusses challenges of mobile networking, including IP address changes and security. It explains how IP addresses serve as both identifiers and locators, prompting the need for separation. Mobile IP is introduced as a solution with home addresses and foreign network care-of addresses, requiring minimal changes for incremental deployment. nodes.title: 5.1 Simple demultiplexer (UDP)

nodes.title: 5.2.1 End-to-End Issues

nodes.title: 5.2.2 Segment Format

nodes.title: Three-Way Handshake

It details silly window syndrome, where small segments cause inefficiency, and solutions: receiver waiting for MSS space before reopening a zero window, delayed ACKs, and sender-side Nagle's algorithm. The TCP_NODELAY option disables Nagle for low-latency applications.

nodes.title: Nagle's Algorithm

nodes.title: 5.2.6 Adaptive Retransmission
Original Algorithm
nodes.summary: This section explains TCP's adaptive retransmission for reliable delivery, focusing on timeout calculation based on expected round-trip time (RTT). The section then introduces the Karn/Partridge algorithm, which identifies a flaw: ACKs acknowledge data receipt, not specific transmissions, causing ambiguity when segments are retransmitted.

nodes.title: Karn/Partridge Algorithm

It then describes the Karn/Partridge algorithm, which addresses ACK ambiguity by not sampling retransmitted segments and introduces exponential backoff for timeouts. Finally, it introduces the Jacobson/Karels algorithm, developed during high network congestion.

nodes.title: Jacobson/Karels Algorithm

It explains the Karn/Partridge algorithm, which avoids sampling RTT for retransmitted segments and uses exponential backoff, and the Jacobson/Karels algorithm, which incorporates RTT variance into timeout calculation using EstimatedRTT and Deviation. Implementation details include integer arithmetic with scaling and clock granularity issues. The text also relates timeouts to congestion control, noting that accurate timeout values prevent unnecessary retransmissions and trigger congestion mechanisms, with a note that Jacobson/Karels is protocol-agnostic.

nodes.title: Implementation

Clock granularity issues in Unix implementations can cause imprecise RTT estimates and delayed timeouts. Retransmission algorithms rely on acknowledgment timeouts, but cumulative ACKs limit sender knowledge about subsequent segments. TCP's byte-stream nature lacks record boundaries, unlike UDP. However, urgent data (URG flag and UrgPtr) and push operations can be used to insert record boundaries, originally designed for out-of-band data but now often repurposed as record markers.
