RTCP's functions are introduced: performance feedback, media stream synchronization, and sender identity conveyance.

nodes.title: 5.4.3 Control Protocol
nodes.summary: This text covers RTP's contributing source for mixers, then details RTCP: its three main functions (performance feedback, media synchronization, and sender identity); packet types (sender/receiver reports, source descriptions, application-specific); bandwidth scaling rules (5% limit, more for senders); sender report contents (time-of-day timestamp, RTP timestamp, cumulative counts); report block statistics (SSRC, loss fraction, total lost, highest sequence, jitter, last timestamp, delay); source description packets with CNAME (user@host) binding to SSRCs; and concludes that RTP/RTCP complexity benefits application designers. A chapter summary describes UDP, TCP (with five algorithms), and request/reply protocols.

Section 5.4 introduces RTP for real-time applications like VoIP and multimedia, distinguishing interactive from streaming needs. It covers requirements such as interoperability, encoding negotiation, timing, synchronization, loss indication, congestion response, frame boundary marking, sender identification, and bandwidth efficiency. The design explains RTP and RTCP using consecutive UDP ports, profiles, formats, Application Level Framing, and the RTP header fields. RTCP's functions include performance feedback, media stream synchronization, and sender identity. Control protocol details cover mixer sources, RTCP packet types, bandwidth scaling, sender reports, report block statistics, and CNAME binding.

nodes.title: 5.5 Summary
nodes.summary: This text covers additional RTP source description packet items like CNAME and user details, notes RTP/RTCP complexity for application flexibility and their Internet success, and summarizes four end-to-end protocols: UDP as a simple demultiplexer, TCP as a reliable byte-stream protocol with sliding window, flow control, and timeout/retransmission algorithms, request/reply RPC protocols with dispatch, matching, reliability, and fragmentation, and multimedia protocols like RTP/RTCP for timing recovery, synchronization, and loss reporting. It concludes that transport protocol design is challenging, requiring adaptation to network and application changes, and discusses transport protocol diversity including SCTP and reusing existing protocols versus creating new ones.

nodes.title: What’s Next: Transport Protocol Diversity
nodes.summary: This chapter summary covers transport protocols for multimedia and real-time applications, detailing RTP and RTCP for timing recovery, stream synchronization, and loss notification for application-specific recovery and congestion avoidance. It discusses the challenges of transport protocol design amid changing network conditions and new applications, weighing reuse versus new protocols like SCTP. It also notes tweaking applications to use TCP, such as RPC over TCP/HTTP, and TCP's growing role in streaming video. The chapter concludes with the Internet hourglass architecture and TCP's potential as the waist. Further reading includes the TCP specification, RPC, and protocol architecture papers.

nodes.title: Further Reading
nodes.summary: The text discusses TCP's dominance as a transport protocol, noting its use for RPC and streaming video due to NAT/firewall traversal, and its potential as part of the Internet's hourglass waist. It includes further reading on TCP, RPC, RTP, SCTP, and performance evaluations, plus references to distributed operating systems' RPC protocols and RTP RFCs. Finally, it lists exercises, starting with a UDP port scenario.

nodes.title: Exercises
nodes.summary: The text covers exercises and references on transport protocols. It cites books and papers on TCP/IP, SCTP, RPC, and RTP, including performance evaluations and timeout algorithms. It lists RFCs and a live reference for protocol information. Exercises address UDP ICMP errors, file transfer protocol design, TCP teardown sequences, TIME_WAIT, sequence number wrap, sliding window design, SYN handling, TCP state transitions, Nagle algorithm, and TCP extensions. Additional exercises cover RPC semantics, NFS performance, SunRPC, RTP timestamping and RTCP reporting, and socket programming experiments.

summary: Chapter 5 covers end-to-end transport protocols for process-to-process communication over best-effort networks. It introduces requirements like reliable, ordered delivery and flow control. It details UDP for simple demultiplexing with ports, TCP for reliable byte streams with sliding windows, adaptive retransmission, and connection management, and RPC for request/reply with SunRPC and DCE-RPC. RTP/RTCP for real-time multimedia handles timing, synchronization, and loss reporting. The chapter concludes with transport protocol diversity, TCP's dominance in the Internet hourglass, further reading, and exercises on protocol design and analysis.

title: Chapter 6. Congestion Control and Resource Allocation

nodes.title: Problem: Allocating Resources
nodes.summary: The text introduces congestion control and resource allocation as a cross-layer problem involving fair sharing of link bandwidth and router buffers among competing users, where excessive contention causes queue overflow and packet drops. It frames resource allocation and congestion control as two sides of the same coin, discussing active allocation versus reactive recovery, with mixed approaches. It notes involvement of hosts and network elements, including queuing disciplines and host pacing. It outlines the chapter's structure: overview, queuing disciplines, TCP congestion control, congestion avoidance, and quality of service, then begins discussing resource allocation issues.

nodes.title: 6.1 Issues in resource allocation
6.1 Issues in resource allocation (intro)
nodes.summary: This text introduces congestion control and resource allocation, discussing trade-offs between precise allocation, reactive congestion control, and mixed approaches. It highlights the roles of hosts and network elements like routers, including queuing disciplines and end-host pacing. The chapter covers an overview, router queuing disciplines, TCP congestion control, congestion avoidance techniques, and quality of service. Section 6.1 examines resource allocation issues, defining resource allocation as meeting application demands for bandwidth and buffer space, and congestion control as preventing or responding to overload. It distinguishes flow control from congestion control and outlines network architecture features relevant to resource allocation.

nodes.title: 6.1.1 Network Model
nodes.summary: This section examines resource allocation in packet-switched networks, involving routers, switches, transport protocols, and signalling. It defines resource allocation as meeting competing demands for bandwidth and buffer space, potentially denying some requests. Congestion control prevents or mitigates overload, often with fairness, and is distinguished from flow control. The network model covers packet-switched networks, bottleneck routers, connectionless flows, soft state, implicit versus explicit flows, and the best-effort service model versus QoS. A taxonomy of resource allocation mechanisms is introduced based on three dimensions.

nodes.title: 6.1.2 Taxonomy
6.1.2 Taxonomy (intro)
nodes.summary: The section discusses resource allocation issues, defining implicit versus explicit flows and noting flows lack end-to-end semantics. It covers the best-effort service model versus QoS guarantees, then presents a taxonomy of allocation mechanisms: router-centric versus host-centric, and reservation-based versus feedback-based. It explains how routers or hosts manage congestion, how reservations request capacity and may be rejected, and how feedback can be explicit or implicit.

nodes.title: Router-Centric versus Host-Centric
nodes.summary: Resource allocation mechanisms are classified into router-centric versus host-centric and reservation-based versus feedback-based approaches. Router-centric designs have routers decide packet forwarding, dropping, and informing hosts of allowed send rates, while host-centric designs have end hosts observe network conditions and adjust behavior. These groups are not mutually exclusive. Reservation-based systems require hosts to request capacity, with routers allocating resources or rejecting requests, analogous to a busy signal. Feedback-based approaches let hosts send data without reservation and adjust rates based on explicit or implicit feedback, such as congestion messages or packet losses.

nodes.title: Reservation-Based versus Feedback-Based
nodes.summary: Resource allocation mechanisms are classified in three ways: router-centric vs. host-centric (where the burden of congestion management falls), noting they are not mutually exclusive; reservation-based vs. feedback-based (reservations require router-centric, feedback can be explicit or implicit and may be router- or host-centric, and reservations can be made by administrators), and window-based vs. rate-based (window advertisement for flow control and resource allocation, rate-based for multimedia, applied to both flow and congestion control).

nodes.title: Window Based versus Rate Based
nodes.summary: The text examines resource allocation issues, starting with reservation-based systems that are router-centric, where routers track capacity and enforce host reservations, versus feedback-based systems that can be router- or host-centric, with explicit or implicit feedback. Reservations can also be made by network administrators. It then contrasts window-based and rate-based mechanisms, noting their use in flow and congestion control, with window-based approaches like TCP and rate-based approaches suited for multimedia and QoS. The taxonomy suggests two prevalent strategies: best-effort networks using feedback and window-based control with host responsibility, and QoS networks using reservations and rate-based control with router involvement. Finally, it introduces evaluation criteria for assessing resource allocation mechanisms.

nodes.title: Summary of Resource Allocation Taxonomy
nodes.summary: The text discusses rate-based flow characterization in reservation-based systems, where senders reserve bandwidth and routers check support. It summarizes resource allocation taxonomy, noting that while eight strategies are possible, two prevail: best-effort service (using feedback and window-based information, with end-host responsibility, as in the Internet) and QoS-based service (using reservations, rate-based, with significant router involvement). It then introduces evaluation criteria for resource allocation mechanisms, focusing on effectiveness and fairness.

The section discusses resource allocation, defining implicit versus explicit flows lacking end-to-end semantics, and contrasting best-effort versus QoS guarantees. It presents a taxonomy of allocation mechanisms: router-centric versus host-centric, and reservation-based versus feedback-based. Router-centric designs have routers manage congestion, while host-centric designs have hosts adjust behavior; these are not mutually exclusive. Reservation-based systems require capacity requests that may be rejected, while feedback-based systems adjust rates using explicit or implicit feedback. Additionally, it covers window-based versus rate-based mechanisms, noting their use in flow and congestion control. Two prevailing strategies emerge: best-effort networks using feedback and window-based control with host responsibility, and QoS networks using reservations and rate-based control with router involvement. Evaluation criteria for resource allocation mechanisms, focusing on effectiveness and fairness, are introduced.

nodes.title: 6.1.3 Evaluation Criteria
6.1.3 Evaluation Criteria (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers rate-based flow characterization for reservations, resource allocation taxonomy contrasting best-effort (feedback-driven, window-based, end-host responsibility) and QoS (reservation-based, router-involved, rate-expressed) models, and evaluation criteria using throughput and delay, including the power metric (throughput/delay) based on M/M/1 queues, its limitations, and the goal to maximize it by operating at the peak of the power curve.

nodes.title: Effective Resource Allocation
nodes.summary: The text covers effective and fair resource allocation in networking. It discusses the trade-off between throughput and delay, introducing network power (throughput/delay) as a metric, with a power curve showing optimal load. It notes limitations of power, including M/M/1 assumptions and single-flow focus. It also compares to timesharing thrashing, emphasizes stability to avoid congestion collapse, and introduces fairness as an additional criterion.

nodes.title: Fair Resource Allocation
nodes.summary: This text covers resource allocation and congestion control. It discusses a throughput/delay power curve, noting peak efficiency and the risk of congestion collapse under heavy load, emphasizing stability. Fair resource allocation is examined, including reservation-based unfairness, equal versus fair shares with varying path lengths, and Jain's fairness index. The text then introduces queuing disciplines: FIFO (first-in, first-out) with tail drop when buffers fill, and mentions fair queuing (FQ) as another approach. It includes a lab on queues.

This section covers rate-based flow characterization for reservations and resource allocation models, contrasting best-effort and QoS approaches. Evaluation criteria include throughput, delay, and the power metric (throughput/delay), with limitations due to M/M/1 assumptions and single-flow focus. It discusses effective and fair allocation, the throughput-delay trade-off, power curve optimal load, stability to prevent congestion collapse, fairness criteria including Jain's fairness index, and queuing disciplines like FIFO with tail drop and fair queuing, plus a related lab.

Section 6.1 introduces resource allocation and congestion control, covering trade-offs, host and network roles, and distinguishing flow control from congestion control. It defines resource allocation as meeting bandwidth and buffer demands, and congestion control as preventing or responding to overload. The network model discusses packet-switched networks, bottleneck routers, connectionless flows, soft state, implicit/explicit flows, and best-effort versus QoS. A taxonomy classifies mechanisms as router- versus host-centric, reservation- versus feedback-based, and window- versus rate-based, leading to best-effort and QoS strategies. Evaluation criteria include throughput, delay, power metric, stability, and fairness (e.g., Jain's index), with queuing disciplines like FIFO with tail drop and fair queuing, plus a related lab.

nodes.title: 6.2 Queuing disciplines
6.2.1 FIFO
nodes.summary: The text explains how fairness index drops when traffic is uneven, and introduces queuing disciplines. It details FIFO queuing with tail drop, noting they are separable scheduling and drop policies. It describes priority queuing, where multiple FIFO queues serve higher priorities first, risking starvation, and its use for routing updates. It then introduces fair queuing as a response to FIFO's lack of flow discrimination, setting up further discussion.

nodes.title: 6.2.2 Fair Queuing
6.2.2 Fair Queuing (intro)
nodes.summary: The text discusses queuing disciplines: priority queuing, where packets are marked with priority and served from highest-priority queue first, but can starve lower priorities, requiring limits or economic pushback; used for critical packets like routing updates. Fair queuing (FQ) addresses FIFO's lack of discrimination by maintaining per-flow queues and round-robin service, preventing ill-behaved flows from dominating and enforcing fairness. FQ doesn't signal sources but segregates traffic. Complications include variable packet lengths; bit-by-bit round-robin is simulated using finishing times (Fi = max(Fi-1, Ai) + Pi) with a virtual clock advancing based on active flows. Packets are sequenced by lowest finish time, allowing shorter packets to be inserted ahead, but no preemption of in-progress transmissions. An example illustrates FQ operation.

nodes.title: Output
nodes.summary: This section covers fair queuing (FQ) and weighted fair queuing (WFQ) for congestion control and resource allocation. It explains computing finish times (Fi) using a virtual clock, selecting packets with lowest timestamps, and non-preemption limitations. FQ ensures work conservation and minimum bandwidth guarantees, while WFQ assigns weights for proportional bandwidth allocation. The text discusses queue management, drop policies, reservation-based models, and the system design principle of separating policy and mechanism. It also introduces TCP congestion control's end-to-end strategy without reservations.

This section covers fair queuing (FQ) and weighted fair queuing (WFQ) for congestion control and resource allocation. It begins by discussing priority queuing and its starvation issue, then introduces FQ to provide per-flow queueing and round-robin service, preventing ill-behaved flows from dominating. It explains the bit-by-bit round-robin simulation using finish times (Fi = max(Fi-1, Ai) + Pi) and a virtual clock, with packets sequenced by lowest finish time, though non-preemption applies. WFQ extends FQ by assigning weights for proportional bandwidth allocation. The section also addresses queue management, drop policies, reservation-based models, and the design principle of separating policy and mechanism, concluding with TCP congestion control's end-to-end approach without reservations.

Section 6.2 covers queuing disciplines. It explains that fairness index drops with uneven traffic. FIFO queuing with tail drop separates scheduling and drop policies. Priority queuing uses multiple FIFO queues, serving higher priorities first, risking starvation, and is used for routing updates. Fair queuing (FQ) addresses FIFO's lack of flow discrimination, providing per-flow queueing and round-robin service to prevent ill-behaved flows from dominating. It uses bit-by-bit round-robin simulation with finish times (Fi = max(Fi-1, Ai) + Pi) and a virtual clock, sequencing packets by lowest finish time, with non-preemption. Weighted fair queuing (WFQ) extends FQ with weights for proportional bandwidth. The section also covers queue management, drop policies, reservation-based models, separating policy and mechanism, and TCP congestion control's end-to-end approach without reservations.

nodes.title: 6.3 TCP congestion control
6.3 TCP congestion control (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers WFQ, where flows or classes get weighted bandwidth shares, possibly based on IP header bits for Differentiated Services. Routers must learn weights via configuration or signaling, leading to reservation-based models. It highlights separating policy and mechanism. Then, TCP congestion control is introduced: its strategy, history by Van Jacobson, addressing congestion collapse, self-clocking via ACKs, and dynamic capacity adjustment. The text notes multiple TCP variants and describes CongestionWindow as a state variable, with additive increase/multiplicative decrease as the first mechanism, though mechanisms work together.

nodes.title: 6.3.1 Additive Increase/Multiplicative Decrease
6.3.1 Additive Increase/Multiplicative Decrease (intro)
nodes.summary: This text covers TCP congestion control, including its introduction by Van Jacobson in the late 1980s to address congestion collapse. It explains the self-clocking principle where ACKs pace transmission, the use of the CongestionWindow variable, and the AIMD mechanism. It details how timeouts signal congestion, leading to multiplicative decrease (halving the window). The text also notes that TCP congestion control comprises multiple mechanisms, has various implementations, and replaces AdvertisedWindow with the minimum of CongestionWindow and AdvertisedWindow in effective window calculation.

nodes.title: Source
nodes.summary: The text covers TCP congestion control, focusing on AIMD's multiplicative decrease and additive increase, with the congestion window not falling below one MSS. It details additive increase's linear growth via per-ACK increments, the sawtooth pattern, and AIMD's stability rationale. It addresses TCP over wireless, where packet loss from bit errors is misread as congestion, and discusses solutions like FEC, link-layer retransmission, connection splitting, and loss differentiation. It also covers TCP's timeout mechanism and slow start's exponential growth from one packet, contrasting it with additive increase and explaining the historical naming.

This section explains TCP congestion control via AIMD, introduced by Van Jacobson to prevent congestion collapse. It covers self-clocking, CongestionWindow, and effective window calculation. Timeouts trigger multiplicative decrease (halving window), while additive increase grows linearly per ACK, producing a sawtooth pattern. The window never drops below one MSS. It addresses AIMD stability, TCP over wireless misinterpreting bit errors as congestion, and solutions like FEC, link-layer retransmission, splitting, and loss differentiation. It also contrasts slow start's exponential growth with additive increase and explains its historical naming.

nodes.title: 6.3.2 Slow Start
nodes.summary: This text covers TCP congestion control, detailing slow start and fast retransmit/recovery. It explains that timeouts depend on average RTT and its standard deviation, sampled once per RTT. Slow start exponentially increases the congestion window from one packet, contrasting with additive increase and the original TCP behavior that sent full windows at once. It discusses use cases: connection start and after timeouts, including CongestionThreshold and code logic. A trace shows congestion window changes over time. It addresses packet loss during initial slow start, trade-offs between aggressive and conservative growth, and the quick-start mechanism. Finally, it introduces fast retransmit as an enhancement to regular timeouts due to coarse-grained timers.

nodes.title: 6.3.3 Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery
nodes.summary: The text covers TCP congestion control enhancements: quick-start, where senders request higher initial rates via SYN, requiring router cooperation; fast retransmit, using duplicate ACKs to retransmit lost packets sooner, eliminating about half of coarse timeouts and improving throughput by 20%; fast recovery, which halves the congestion window instead of slow start after fast retransmit; and challenges for high-speed TCP, including the throughput formula, HighSpeed TCP, CUBIC, FAST TCP, and proposals for dramatic changes. It also introduces congestion avoidance, which predicts and avoids congestion rather than reacting after it occurs.

Section 6.3 covers TCP congestion control, beginning with WFQ and Differentiated Services before introducing TCP's strategy, history by Van Jacobson, and the CongestionWindow state variable. Subsection 6.3.1 explains Additive Increase/Multiplicative Decrease (AIMD) for congestion collapse prevention, including self-clocking, effective window, timeouts, sawtooth patterns, stability, wireless issues, and slow start contrast. Subsection 6.3.2 details slow start's exponential growth, timeout calculation, CongestionThreshold, traces, and quick-start. Subsection 6.3.3 covers quick-start, fast retransmit/recovery, high-speed TCP variants (HighSpeed, CUBIC, FAST), and congestion avoidance.

nodes.title: 6.4 Congestion-avoidance mechanisms
6.4 Congestion-avoidance mechanisms (intro)
nodes.summary: The text discusses TCP congestion control proposals: HighSpeed TCP for high bandwidth-delay environments, CUBIC as Linux default, Quick-Start for faster ramp-up, and FAST TCP for congestion anticipation. It introduces congestion avoidance, contrasting it with congestion control. The DECbit mechanism is detailed: routers set a congestion bit when average queue length exceeds 1, derived from busy/idle cycles, and sources adjust their congestion window based on the fraction of marked packets, increasing it if less than 50% are marked. The text also mentions other proposals and ongoing work.

nodes.title: 6.4.1 DECbit
nodes.summary: Section 6.4 covers three congestion-avoidance mechanisms. DECbit, the first, uses routers that set a congestion bit in packets based on average queue length, with destinations echoing it in ACKs so sources adjust window sizes. The second, Random Early Detection (RED), also monitors router queues but implicitly notifies sources by dropping packets early, designed for TCP. The third mechanism, though not detailed, avoids congestion purely from end nodes, contrasting with the router-assisted approaches.

nodes.title: 6.4.2 Random Early Detection (RED)
nodes.summary: The text covers congestion control mechanisms in computer networks, focusing on DECbit and Random Early Detection (RED). DECbit uses router monitoring and explicit notifications to adjust source congestion windows. RED implicitly notifies sources by dropping packets early, using an average queue length and thresholds (MinThreshold, MaxThreshold) with a calculated drop probability to avoid congestion and tail drop. The text details RED's algorithm, including weighted running average, probability calculation, and parameter tuning. It also discusses Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN), source-based congestion avoidance using RTT measurements, and the unresponsive flow problem.

nodes.title: 6.4.3 Source-Based Congestion Avoidance
nodes.summary: The text covers congestion-avoidance mechanisms, including RED's Weight parameter and the unresponsive flow problem. It then details source-based congestion avoidance, discussing algorithms that use RTT, window size, and throughput changes. TCP Vegas is explained in depth: its use of BaseRTT, ExpectedRate, ActualRate, and α/β thresholds to maintain extra data. A sidebar compares TCP Tahoe, Reno, and Vegas, noting TCP's evolution. Finally, it introduces quality of service and real-time applications, arguing that best-effort service is insufficient for timeliness.

Section 6.4 covers congestion-avoidance mechanisms: DECbit uses routers to set congestion bits based on average queue length, with sources adjusting windows via ACK feedback. RED implicitly notifies sources by dropping packets early using average queue length and thresholds, and ECN is discussed. Source-based avoidance uses RTT, window size, and throughput changes, with TCP Vegas detailed. The unresponsive flow problem and a comparison of TCP Tahoe, Reno, and Vegas are included, ending with quality of service and real-time applications.

nodes.title: 6.5 Quality of service
6.5 Quality of service (intro)
nodes.summary: Section 6.5 covers Quality of Service (QoS), explaining that real-time applications like voice and video need timely delivery assurances beyond best-effort service, which cannot guarantee timeliness due to retransmission limitations. It introduces QoS as a superset service model offering different packet treatments. Section 6.5.1 discusses application requirements, dividing applications into real-time and non-real-time (elastic) types, with the latter including telnet, FTP, email, and web browsing, which can tolerate delay.

nodes.title: 6.5.1 Application Requirements
6.5.1 Application Requirements (intro)
nodes.summary: The text introduces quality of service (QoS) as a new service model for real-time applications needing higher network assurances, noting it's a superset of best-effort service. It questions if the Internet already supports real-time apps like Skype, explaining best-effort is often adequate but lacks guarantees. It then covers application requirements, dividing applications into real-time and non-real-time (elastic) types, with examples like telnet, FTP, email, and web browsing. A real-time audio example illustrates sample generation, packet transmission, playback times, and the worthlessness of late data, plus the need for receiver buffering to handle variable delays.

nodes.title: Real-Time Audio Example
nodes.summary: The text uses a real-time audio application to illustrate real-time constraints: samples digitized and packetized must be played back at a fixed rate; late data is useless. It explains variable network delay due to queues causes packets to arrive at different times, so a playback buffer is used with a playback point to absorb jitter. A 300 ms delay limit is noted for conversation. Delay distribution data shows 97% of packets arrive within 100 ms, but a long tail means some arrive after 200 ms. It introduces a taxonomy of real-time applications based on Clark, Braden, Shenker, and Zhang.

nodes.title: Taxonomy of Real-Time Applications
nodes.summary: The text covers network delay variability for real-time applications using Figure 6.22, showing that 97% of packets had latency of 100 ms or less but long tails require over 200 ms for all packets. It then presents a taxonomy from Clark et al. (Figure 6.23) categorizing applications as elastic or real-time, with real-time subdivided into tolerant vs. intolerant of loss and nonadaptive vs. adaptive, where adaptive includes delay-adaptive (adjusting playback point) and rate-adaptive (trading bit rate for quality). Examples include audio, robot control, and video. Finally, it introduces the need for a richer QoS service model to support diverse application requirements.

nodes.title: Approaches to QoS Support
nodes.summary: The text contrasts delay-adaptive and rate-adaptive real-time applications, explaining playback point adjustment and its trade-offs. It then introduces QoS support approaches, categorizing them as fine-grained (Integrated Services, RSVP, ATM) and coarse-grained (Differentiated Services). Integrated Services service classes and RSVP reservations are briefly described, with a mention of end-host support for real-time streams.

This section introduces Quality of Service (QoS) as a service model for real-time applications, explaining that best-effort service often suffices but lacks guarantees. It covers application requirements, dividing applications into real-time and non-real-time (elastic) types. A real-time audio example illustrates sampling, packetization, playback, variable network delay, and receiver buffering (playback buffer) to handle jitter, noting a 300 ms delay limit for conversation. A taxonomy of real-time applications is presented: elastic vs. real-time, with real-time divided into loss-tolerant/intolerant and nonadaptive/adaptive (delay-adaptive, rate-adaptive), with examples. Finally, it introduces QoS support approaches: fine-grained (Integrated Services, RSVP, ATM) and coarse-grained (Differentiated Services).

nodes.title: 6.5.2 Integrated Services (RSVP)
Service Classes
nodes.summary: The text introduces quality of service (QoS) approaches categorized as fine-grained (for individual applications or flows) and coarse-grained (for aggregated traffic). Fine-grained includes Integrated Services (IntServ) with RSVP and ATM's QoS; coarse-grained includes Differentiated Services, widely deployed. It then focuses on IntServ, developed by IETF in 1995-97, detailing service classes: guaranteed service for intolerant applications requiring bounded delay, and controlled load for tolerant, adaptive applications emulating a lightly loaded network via WFQ and admission control. It outlines mechanisms for implementing these services, noting best-effort requires only destination, while real-time service requires additional qualitative or quantitative information. The discussion also mentions end-host support for real-time streams independent of QoS deployment.

nodes.title: Overview of Mechanisms
nodes.summary: The text discusses IETF service classes: guaranteed service ensures no packet arrives after playback time, while controlled load emulates a lightly loaded network for tolerant applications using WFQ and admission control. It contrasts best-effort with real-time services, introduces the flowspec (TSpec and RSpec) to describe flow traffic and requested service, and outlines key mechanisms: admission control, resource reservation, and packet scheduling. It also notes that other services were specified but not standardized, and that guaranteed, controlled load, and best-effort cover many applications.

nodes.title: Flowspecs
nodes.summary: This section covers quality of service mechanisms: flowspec (TSpec for traffic characteristics and RSpec for requested service), admission control for deciding if new flows can be admitted, resource reservation for signaling, and packet scheduling for managing queues. It explains token bucket filters for describing bandwidth variability, with examples of two flows. Admission control depends on service type and queuing discipline, differs from policing, and involves policy considerations. Policing ensures flows conform to TSpec, with options like dropping or tagging nonconforming packets.

nodes.title: Admission Control
nodes.summary: The text covers admission control, which decides whether to admit a new flow based on its TSpec and RSpec, considering available resources and impact on existing flows. It contrasts admission control with policing, which enforces per-packet conformance to TSpec. Policy considerations in admission control are mentioned. It then introduces reservation protocols, focusing on RSVP for connectionless networks, highlighting its use of soft state for robustness and its receiver-oriented approach to support multicast and unicast flows, differing from traditional connection-oriented signaling.

nodes.title: Reservation Protocol
nodes.summary: This section covers Quality of Service (QoS) and RSVP, a receiver-oriented reservation protocol for connectionless networks. It explains RSVP's soft state mechanism, support for multicast and unicast flows, and how it handles reservations via PATH and RESV messages. It details reservation merging for multiple receivers, multiple sender handling, and different reservation styles. It describes robustness to router/link failures through periodic refreshes and timeouts. Finally, it outlines packet classifying (using five fields) and scheduling to deliver requested services.

nodes.title: Packet Classifying and Scheduling
nodes.summary: The text discusses merging RSVP reservations to meet multiple receivers' needs, handling multiple senders by collecting TSpecs with application-specific merging (e.g., audioconference limits), and various reservation styles. It then covers packet classifying and scheduling for delivering requested service. Finally, it addresses RSVP and Integrated Services deployment: limited due to scalability, but RSVP is widely used for MPLS traffic engineering, with potential revival via aggregate reservations, driven by QoS-demanding applications, admission control benefits, and high-bandwidth applications.

nodes.title: Rsvp and Integrated Services Deployment
nodes.summary: The text examines RSVP and Integrated Services deployment, noting limited adoption due to scalability concerns, but RSVP's use for MPLS traffic engineering. It suggests a potential resurgence driven by QoS-demanding applications like VoIP and video, admission control benefits, and IETF standardization of aggregate reservations. It then covers packet classification mapping flow-specific header info to class identifiers, and queue management disciplines like weighted fair queuing for guaranteed service and simpler schemes for controlled load, emphasizing the need for overall queue management across services. Finally, it reiterates scalability issues as a key reason ISPs hesitated to deploy the architecture.

nodes.title: Scalability Issues
nodes.summary: The text covers packet classification based on header information to determine queue handling, contrasting FIFO queues with sophisticated queue management for differentiated services. It discusses scheduling, including weighted fair queuing for guaranteed service and aggregated approaches for controlled load, and the need to manage multiple services. Scalability issues with Integrated Services and RSVP are examined, noting per-flow state challenges. Differentiated Services (DiffServ) is introduced, allocating resources to traffic classes, using a packet bit to mark premium packets, per-hop behaviors (PHBs), DSCPs in the TOS byte, and the Expedited Forwarding PHB for minimal delay and loss.

nodes.title: The Expedited Forwarding (EF) PHB
nodes.summary: The text discusses quality of service mechanisms for marking premium packets using a header bit, addressing who sets the bit and router responses. It introduces per-hop behaviors (PHBs) standardized by IETF, using six-bit DiffServ code points from the TOS byte. It details the Expedited Forwarding (EF) PHB, which requires rate limiting at domain edges and can be implemented via strict priority or weighted fair queuing, and the Assured Forwarding (AF) PHB, based on RIO with separate drop curves for 'in' and 'out' traffic, dropping 'out' packets first under low congestion.

nodes.title: The Assured Forwarding (AF) PHB
nodes.summary: The text covers Quality of Service, focusing on EF and AF per-hop behaviors. EF rate limiting is described to prevent overload, with implementation via strict priority or weighted fair queuing. AF uses RIO or WRED with in/out marking and drop probability curves based on profiles. RIO maintains packet order and generalizes to WRED using DSCP for multiple classes. A third DiffServ method uses DSCP for weighted fair queuing. The text concludes with DiffServ's quiet success in enterprise VoIP and business services, noting it allocates but doesn't create bandwidth.

nodes.title: THE QUIET SUCCESS OF DIFFSERV
nodes.summary: The text discusses DiffServ's quiet success despite earlier pessimism, noting its deployment in enterprise IP telephony, residential VoIP, and national telephone networks, and the importance of QoS assurance and bandwidth allocation. It covers WFQ-based approaches and assured service with code points and drop preferences. ATM QoS is examined, including its five service classes (CBR, VBR-rt, VBR-nrt, ABR, UBR) and ABR's explicit congestion feedback via RM cells. The section concludes with equation-based congestion control for real-time applications, proposing TCP-like congestion control on unreliable protocols like UDP.

This section covers Integrated Services (IntServ) and RSVP for QoS. It details service classes: guaranteed service with bounded delay and controlled load emulating lightly loaded networks. Mechanisms include flowspecs (TSpec and RSpec), admission control, resource reservation, and packet scheduling with token bucket filters. RSVP is a receiver-oriented protocol using soft state, PATH/RESV messages, reservation merging, and robustness. Packet classification and scheduling are discussed. Deployment is limited due to scalability, but RSVP is used for MPLS traffic engineering and may revive with aggregate reservations. Scalability issues lead to Differentiated Services (DiffServ), with per-hop behaviors like Expedited Forwarding and Assured Forwarding. DiffServ has seen quiet success. ATM QoS and equation-based congestion control are also covered.

nodes.title: 6.5.4 Equation-Based Congestion Control
nodes.summary: The text covers ATM QoS mechanisms like rate decay and proprietary switch algorithms for throughput and low delay/loss, noting common mechanisms with IP QoS such as admission control, scheduling, token bucket policers, and explicit congestion feedback. It introduces equation-based congestion control for real-time applications, contrasting TCP's unsuitability due to reliability and sawtooth behavior with TCP-friendly algorithms that adapt the congestion window slowly to ensure fairness via an equation relating rate to RTT and loss rate. The summary reiterates resource allocation aspects: congestion control and QoS, end-node responsibility, router queuing disciplines (WFQ, RED, DECbit), and QoS approaches IntServ/RSVP and DiffServ, with DiffServ more deployed but neither widely in the public Internet.

Section 6.5 covers Quality of Service (QoS) for real-time applications like voice and video, which need timely delivery beyond best-effort service. It explains application requirements, dividing them into real-time and non-real-time (elastic) types, and discusses jitter, playback buffering, and a taxonomy of real-time applications (loss-tolerant/intolerant, adaptive/nonadaptive). QoS support approaches include fine-grained (Integrated Services, RSVP, ATM) and coarse-grained (Differentiated Services). It details IntServ/RSVP mechanisms (flowspecs, admission control, reservation, scheduling), DiffServ per-hop behaviors (Expedited and Assured Forwarding), ATM QoS, and equation-based congestion control for TCP-friendly real-time traffic. Deployment challenges and scalability are noted.

nodes.title: 6.6 Summary
nodes.summary: The text summarizes resource allocation in networking, covering congestion control mechanisms for the best-effort Internet (like TCP's feedback and router queuing disciplines such as WFQ, RED, DECbit) and quality of service approaches (Integrated Services with RSVP and Differentiated Services). It discusses deployment challenges for IntServ and DiffServ, the trade-off between network intelligence and end-host responsibility, the end-to-end principle, and trends like Skype's overlay routing and rate adaptation. It also poses questions about future QoS options and the evolving role of end systems in managing quality of service.

nodes.title: What’s Next: Refactoring The Network
nodes.summary: The text discusses network congestion control and resource allocation, comparing reservation-based and feedback-based strategies, and examining the role of end hosts versus network intelligence. It covers Differentiated Services as a middle ground between Integrated Services and minimal network intelligence, and trends like Skype's end-system QoS management using rate adaptation and overlay routing. It also includes a further reading list of seminal papers on flow control, fair queuing, congestion avoidance, RED, integrated services, and QoS.

nodes.title: Further Reading
nodes.summary: The text covers further reading on congestion control and resource allocation, listing key papers on flow control, fair queuing, congestion avoidance, RED, Integrated Services, and Differentiated Services. It discusses TCP variants like Vegas, FAST, CUBIC, and HighSpeed TCP, plus ECN, active queue management, XCP, and packet scheduling. It also mentions TCP-friendly congestion control, DCCP, and real-time application performance. The exercises ask about flow definitions, alternative TCP design models, and throughput/delay/power curves for Ethernet.

nodes.title: Exercises
nodes.summary: This text covers network congestion control and resource allocation, including exercises on fair and weighted fair queuing, TCP congestion control algorithms (Reno, Vegas), RED gateways, ECN, token bucket filters, RSVP reservations, and TCP-friendly rate control for real-time applications. It also discusses flow definitions, host-centric vs. router-centric models, throughput-delay-power curves, fairness index calculations, dropping policies, and the transition to end-to-end data encoding, emphasizing message format agreement and efficient encoding.

summary: Chapter 6 covers congestion control and resource allocation as a cross-layer problem involving fair bandwidth and buffer sharing. It introduces resource allocation issues, flow vs. congestion control, and evaluation metrics like fairness. Queuing disciplines (FIFO, priority, fair, weighted fair) and queue management (RED, DECbit, ECN) are explained. The chapter ends with a summary, future trends, further reading, and exercises.

title: Chapter 7. End-to-End Data

nodes.title: Problem: What Do We Do With the Data?
nodes.summary: The text introduces end-to-end data encoding, emphasizing agreement on presentation formats for data like integers, arrays, and multimedia (MPEG, JPEG). It covers encoding efficiency, compression, and the balance between redundancy for error correction and compression for efficiency, referencing Shannon. It notes that compression impacts network design and protocol adaptation. Presentation formatting and compression are data manipulation functions requiring per-byte processing, affecting throughput. The section then defines presentation formatting, including encoding (marshalling) and decoding (unmarshalling), with examples from RPC, and previews Sections 7.1 and 7.2 on traditional and multimedia data encoding.

nodes.title: 7.1 Presentation Formatting
7.1 Presentation Formatting (intro)
nodes.summary: The text discusses presentation formatting, the transformation of application data into a network-transmittable form. Encoding (marshalling) and decoding (unmarshalling) are defined, with the former sometimes called argument marshalling from RPC. Challenges in marshalling arise from differences in data representation across computers, including floating-point formats (IEEE 754 vs. nonstandard), integer sizes (16-bit, 32-bit, 64-bit), and byte order (big-endian vs. little-endian, with examples like MIPS, PowerPC, and Intel x86). Additionally, variations in programming languages and compiler-specific memory layout (e.g., padding) make directly transmitting structures unreliable. Figures illustrate encoding/decoding and big-endian vs. little-endian byte order for an integer.

nodes.title: 7.1.1 Taxonomy
7.1.1 Taxonomy (intro)
nodes.summary: The text explains why marshalling is challenging: computers use different data representations, such as IEEE 754 vs. nonstandard floating-point formats, different integer sizes (16-bit, 32-bit, 64-bit), and big-endian vs. little-endian byte orders (e.g., MIPS and PowerPC vs. Intel x86), illustrated with integer 34,677,374. Compilers also vary in structure layout and padding, and applications may be written in different languages. A taxonomy classifies marshalling systems by data types: base types (integers, floats, characters, ordinals, Booleans) requiring representation conversion; flat types (structures, arrays) needing padding removal; and complex types (using pointers, like trees) requiring serialization to flatten memory addresses.

nodes.title: Data Types
nodes.summary: Section 7.1 covers presentation formatting and argument marshalling. It introduces a taxonomy addressing data types and conversion strategy. Data types are classified into three levels: base types (integers, floats, characters, ordinals, Booleans) requiring representation conversion like endianness; flat types (structures, arrays) requiring packing to remove compiler-inserted padding; and complex types (pointer-based, e.g., trees) requiring serialization/flattening. The marshalling task thus involves converting, packing, and linearizing to form a contiguous message, as illustrated in Figure 7.3. Two conversion strategies are discussed: canonical intermediate form (external representation, e.g., big-endian, with sender/receiver translation) and receiver-makes-right.

nodes.title: Conversion Strategy
nodes.summary: The text discusses argument marshalling, covering conversion of base types, packing structures, and linearizing complex data structures into a contiguous message (Figure 7.3). It details conversion strategies: canonical intermediate form (external representation, e.g., big-endian, requiring each host to convert to/from one format) and receiver-makes-right (sender uses internal format, receiver converts, leading to an N-by-N solution). It notes trade-offs, including efficiency for same-architecture communication and a proposed hybrid option. Finally, it introduces the third issue of how receivers identify data types via tagged versus untagged approaches, defining tags and their role in decoding.

nodes.title: Tags
nodes.summary: The text discusses presentation formatting strategies: receiver-makes-right (N-by-N conversion problem), canonical intermediate form (single external representation), and a hybrid approach based on sender knowing receiver architecture via name server or test case. It covers tagged vs. untagged data for receiver decoding, detailing type, length, and architecture tags, with untagged relying on preprogrammed knowledge and often using length tags for variable-length arrays. The untagged approach enables true end-to-end formatting, preventing intermediate interpretation. Finally, stubs are defined as code implementing argument marshalling for RPC, marshalling on client side and unmarshalling on server side, either interpreted or compiled.

nodes.title: Stubs
nodes.summary: The text covers tagged message encoding, including type, length, and architecture tags, and depicts a 32-bit integer example. It contrasts untagged approaches, where receivers decode based on preprogrammed knowledge, noting breakdowns with variable-length arrays. It highlights that untagged formatting is truly end-to-end, preventing intermediate agent interpretation. Stubs for RPC argument marshalling are explained, covering client and server sides, with compiled stubs (efficient, common) vs. interpreted stubs (flexible). Examples of network data representations—XDR, ASN.1, and NDR—are introduced, illustrating with the integer base type.

nodes.title: XDR
nodes.summary: The text covers presentation formatting, comparing compilation-based (efficient, compiled stubs) and interpretation-based (flexible, interpreted stubs) approaches for RPC stubs. It introduces XDR, ASN.1, and NDR as network data representations, detailing XDR's use in SunRPC: it supports the C type system (except function pointers), uses a canonical intermediate form without tags (except array lengths), and compiled stubs. XDR integers are 32-bit big-endian two's complement; variable-length arrays have a 4-byte length prefix; structures are encoded in declaration order; data is padded to 4 bytes except characters. An example C structure and XDR encoding routine are shown, along with performance considerations. ASN.1 is briefly introduced as an ISO standard.

nodes.title: ASN.1
nodes.summary: The text covers presentation formatting in network data encoding: XDR's encoding/decoding routines, rpcgen stub generation, and performance tied to memory bandwidth or CPU. It introduces ASN.1 with BER, its tag-length-value triple, length encoding for values under 128 bytes and 128+ bytes, nesting for compound types, and inefficiencies versus XDR. NDR is described as using receiver-makes-right, architecture tags, IDL compilation, and a 4-byte architecture tag defining integer, character, and float representations.

nodes.title: NDR
nodes.summary: The text covers ASN.1 BER length encoding, explaining 1-byte and multibyte formats with a bit flag for length field size. It details Network Data Representation (NDR) as DCE's receiver-makes-right encoding, including its architecture tag specifying integer, character, and float representations. It then introduces markup languages, specifically HTML for web page display and XML for web server communication, describing XML as a framework for defining tagged data languages and its role in enabling interoperability similar to RPC.

The section on taxonomy explains the challenges of marshalling due to differing data representations, integer sizes, byte orders, compiler padding, and languages. It classifies data types into base (requiring representation conversion), flat (needing packing to remove padding), and complex (requiring serialization/flattening). Conversion strategies include canonical intermediate form, receiver-makes-right, and hybrid approaches. Receiver decoding uses tagged (type, length, architecture tags) versus untagged formats. Stubs implement marshalling for RPC, either compiled or interpreted. Network data representations covered include XDR (canonical, big-endian, no tags except array lengths), ASN.1 BER (tag-length-value, multibyte length encoding), and NDR (receiver-makes-right with architecture tags). Markup languages HTML and XML are introduced for web display and communication.

nodes.title: 7.1.3 Markup Languages (XML)
nodes.summary: The text covers presentation formatting, starting with NDR details (ASCII/EBCDIC character format field, FloatRep byte for IEEE/VAX/Cray/IBM floating-point, reserved bytes). It then introduces markup languages (XML), explaining HTML, XML as a framework for defining languages, XML syntax with nested tag/value pairs, schema (XSD) for data models, and binary alternatives (Fast Infoset, EXI). It also discusses XML namespaces using URIs to avoid name clashes, with namespace prefixes and qualified names. Finally, it mentions multimedia data as a major part of Internet traffic.

Section 7.1 Presentation Formatting covers transforming application data for network transmission via encoding (marshalling) and decoding (unmarshalling). It addresses challenges from differences in floating-point formats, integer sizes, byte order (big-endian vs. little-endian), compiler padding, and programming languages. A taxonomy classifies data types (base, flat, complex) and conversion strategies (canonical intermediate form, receiver-makes-right, hybrid), decoding with tagged vs. untagged formats, and stub implementations. Network representations include XDR, ASN.1 BER, and NDR. Markup languages XML and HTML are introduced, covering XML syntax, schemas (XSD), binary alternatives (Fast Infoset, EXI), namespaces, and multimedia data.

nodes.title: 7.2 Multimedia Data
7.2 Multimedia Data (intro)
nodes.summary: This text covers XML namespaces, including globally unique identifiers, target namespaces, and namespace prefixes, with examples like emp:title. It highlights XML's broad use in web services, office tools, and instant messaging. Then it discusses multimedia data (audio, video, images) as dominant Internet traffic, enabled by compression. It contrasts lossless and lossy compression, noting human perception's role and better compression ratios for lossy. An HDTV example shows reducing 1 Gbps to 10 Mbps. It introduces lossless techniques like Huffman coding and explains when to compress based on processor speed and network bandwidth.

nodes.title: 7.2.1 Lossless Compression Techniques
7.2.1 Lossless Compression Techniques (intro)
nodes.summary: The text discusses multimedia compression, emphasizing its role in Web video popularity. It introduces lossless compression, noting lossy techniques often include lossless steps. It explains Huffman codes for minimizing bits based on symbol probabilities. It analyzes when compression is beneficial, using formulas involving compression/decompression bandwidth (Bc), network bandwidth (Bn), and compression ratio (r), and mentions tradeoffs in lossy compression for different applications. Finally, it describes Run Length Encoding (RLE) as a simple lossless technique, with an example, and notes its utility for some images.

nodes.title: Run Length Encoding
nodes.summary: The text covers multimedia data compression tradeoffs, including a formula for beneficial compression based on bandwidth and compression ratio, considerations for video and lossy compression tradeoffs like medical images versus phone calls. It describes three lossless algorithms: Run Length Encoding (RLE) for faxes and homogeneous images; Differential Pulse Code Modulation (DPCM) using reference symbols for images and audio; and delta encoding, which encodes differences from the previous symbol and can be combined with RLE.

nodes.title: Differential Pulse Code Modulation
nodes.summary: The text covers lossless compression algorithms: RLE, effective for homogeneous regions like scanned text and faxes but can increase size with local variation; DPCM, which encodes differences from a reference symbol, better for digital imagery and audio due to adjacent similarity; delta encoding, similar to DPCM but uses the previous symbol; and dictionary-based methods like Lempel-Ziv (LZ), used in Unix compress and gzip, which replace strings with dictionary indices, optionally adaptive. It then transitions to image representation and compression, mentioning ISO's digital image format.

nodes.title: Dictionary-Based Methods
nodes.summary: The text covers dictionary-based lossless compression, focusing on the Lempel-Ziv algorithm used in compress and gzip commands, explaining how it builds a dictionary of strings and replaces them with indices, such as replacing "compression" with a 15-bit index for a 5-to-1 ratio, and discusses static versus adaptive dictionaries. It then introduces image representation and compression, detailing JPEG and GIF formats. JPEG transforms RGB to YUV color space, subsamples chrominance components for compression, and applies DCT, quantization, and encoding. GIF reduces colors to 8-bit using a 256-color table and applies LZ compression, suitable for logos but not natural scenes. It also discusses color spaces, human perception, and subsampling techniques like 4:2:0.

nodes.title: DCT Phase
nodes.summary: The text details JPEG compression, starting with chrominance subsampling (4:2:0) for 50% data reduction. It outlines three phases: DCT transforms 8x8 blocks into spatial frequencies (DC and AC coefficients), quantization lossily drops insignificant bits using a quantization table, and encoding adds lossless compression. Decompression reverses these phases. The DCT separates gross features from fine detail, while quantization, controlled by a table, determines information loss and compression. An example quantization table is provided.

nodes.title: Quantization Phase
nodes.summary: The text covers JPEG's quantization and encoding phases. Quantization makes compression lossy by dividing DCT coefficients by values from a quantization table, reducing precision, with larger quantums for high-frequency coefficients. It defines the quantization formula, integer rounding, decompression formula, and provides an example. The encoding phase losslessly compresses quantized coefficients using zigzag ordering, run-length encoding on zero coefficients, and Huffman or arithmetic coding.

nodes.title: Encoding Phase
nodes.summary: This text covers JPEG's final compression phases: quantization, where DCT coefficients are divided by quantum values and rounded, often zeroing high-frequency coefficients; decompression as multiplication; and encoding, which uses zigzag ordering, run-length encoding of zeros, Huffman coding, and delta encoding of DC coefficients. It notes JPEG variations affecting compression and fidelity, with typical 30:1 ratios but artifacts at higher ratios. It then introduces MPEG video compression, explaining that video is a sequence of frames and that interframe redundancy must be removed, as simple JPEG compression of each frame is insufficient, even with motion.

This section covers lossless compression techniques, emphasizing their role in multimedia and Web video. It introduces Huffman codes, compression benefit formulas involving bandwidth and ratio, and tradeoffs in lossy compression. Lossless algorithms detailed include Run Length Encoding (RLE) for homogeneous images, Differential Pulse Code Modulation (DPCM) for imagery/audio, delta encoding, and dictionary-based Lempel-Ziv (LZ) used in compress/gzip. It then transitions to image compression, explaining JPEG's RGB to YUV conversion, chrominance subsampling (4:2:0), DCT, quantization, and encoding phases (zigzag, RLE, Huffman), with typical 30:1 ratios. GIF's color reduction and LZ compression are noted. Finally, MPEG video compression and interframe redundancy removal are introduced.

nodes.title: 7.2.3 Video Compression (MPEG)
7.2.3 Video Compression (MPEG) (intro)
nodes.summary: This text covers JPEG and MPEG video compression. For JPEG, it discusses zigzag traversal of quantized coefficients, delta encoding of DC coefficients, compression variations via quantization tables, typical 30:1 ratios, and artifacts. For MPEG, it explains video as successive frames, DCT-based compression, interframe redundancy removal, and frame types: I (intrapicture, self-contained), P (predicted, differences from previous I), and B (bidirectional, interpolated from surrounding I/P frames), with Figure 7.14 showing a frame sequence.

nodes.title: Frame Types
nodes.summary: MPEG video compression uses I, P, and B frames: I frames are self-contained (JPEG-like), P frames depend on previous I frames, and B frames interpolate between past and future reference frames. B frames are decoded using motion vectors and pixel deltas, allowing flexible macroblock encoding. Transmission order differs from display order. MPEG does not define frame ratios or motion estimation techniques, which are computationally expensive and often done offline. Compression ratios typically reach 90:1, with I frames about 30:1 and P/B frames higher.

nodes.title: Effectiveness and Performance
nodes.summary: The text explains MPEG B-frame delta encoding via DCT and quantization, motion estimation for placing macroblocks using motion vectors, and the challenge of finding similar macroblocks to minimize deltas. It notes MPEG's compression ratios: 90:1 typical, up to 150:1; I frames ~30:1, P/B frames 3-5x smaller; without color reduction, 30:1-50:1. Encoding is computationally expensive, often offline, while decoding is mostly software and now supports HDTV. Other standards include ITU-T H.261, H.263 (low bitrate, ISDN, 64-kbps increments) and H.264 (part of MPEG-4). Finally, MPEG defines video stream format but not network packetization, usable for disk storage or TCP streaming.

nodes.title: Other Video Encoding Standards
nodes.summary: The text discusses MPEG video decoding, noting low-cost boards handle YUV color lookup while software manages most decoding, and modern processors support 30fps and HDTV. It introduces other video encoding standards, particularly ITU-T's H series (H.261, H.263, H.264) for real-time multimedia, contrasting their lower bitrate targets for ISDN with MPEG's 1.5 Mbps, though both use DCT, quantization, and interframe compression. Growing device diversity demands innovation. Finally, it addresses transmitting MPEG over networks, emphasizing that MPEG defines video stream format but not packetization, usable for disk storage or stream-oriented networks like TCP.

The section covers MPEG video compression, beginning with a comparison to JPEG, including zigzag traversal, DC coefficient delta encoding, quantization tables, 30:1 compression, and artifacts. It explains MPEG's DCT-based approach, interframe redundancy removal, and the three frame types: I (self-contained), P (predicted from previous I), and B (bidirectional, interpolated). B-frame decoding uses motion vectors and pixel deltas, with transmission order differing from display. MPEG does not define frame ratios or motion estimation, which is computationally expensive and often offline. Compression ratios reach 90:1 (up to 150:1), with I frames ~30:1 and P/B frames smaller. Other standards include ITU-T H.261, H.263, and H.264. MPEG defines video stream format but not network packetization, suitable for disk storage or TCP streaming.

nodes.title: 7.2.4 Transmitting MPEG over a Network
7.2.4 Transmitting MPEG over a Network (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers MPEG video decoding, noting software handles most decoding and modern processors support HD. It introduces other standards like ITU-T H series (H.261, H.263, H.264) for lower bitrates. It details the MPEG-2 main profile nested format: sequence, GOPs, pictures, slices, macroblocks, and headers, highlighting adaptability in frame rate, resolution, and quantization. It discusses transmitting MPEG over networks, packetization for TCP/UDP, and application-level framing. Finally, it explores adaptive video coding, trading quality for bandwidth using feedback and smoothing buffers.

nodes.title: Adaptive Video Coding
nodes.summary: The text covers adaptive video coding, including Application Level Framing to limit packet loss effects, and rate control using smoothing buffers or feedback to adjust compression during congestion. It discusses receiver-driven layered multicast for heterogeneous receivers, handling packet loss by prioritizing I frames, and latency trade-offs in GOP structures for videoconferencing. It also introduces audio compression with MP3, detailing CD-quality audio's 1.41 Mbps bit rate versus telephone-quality 64 kbps, highlighting the need for compression.

nodes.title: 7.2.5 Audio Compression (MP3)
nodes.summary: The text discusses challenges in videoconferencing due to B frames in GOPs causing delays, as B frames depend on subsequent P/I frames, leading to over a quarter-second delay that exceeds human perception thresholds. Motion-JPEG is suggested as an alternative, and GOPs with only prior dependencies like I P P P P I work better for interactive use. It then introduces MP3 audio compression in MPEG, covering its use for movie audio interleaved with video or standalone audio. CD-quality audio details include 44.1 KHz sampling, 16-bit samples, and 1.41 Mbps stereo bit rate, compared to telephone-quality voice at 8 KHz, 8-bit samples, and 64 kbps, highlighting the need for compression for ISDN transmission.

This section covers transmitting MPEG video over networks, including decoding, standards like ITU-T H series, and the MPEG-2 main profile nested format. It details packetization for TCP/UDP, application-level framing, and adaptive video coding with rate control, smoothing buffers, feedback, and receiver-driven layered multicast. It addresses packet loss prioritization and latency trade-offs in GOP structures for videoconferencing, suggesting Motion-JPEG as an alternative. Finally, it introduces MP3 audio compression, comparing CD-quality audio at 1.41 Mbps to telephone-quality at 64 kbps and highlighting the need for compression.

nodes.title: 7.2.5 Audio Compression (MP3)
nodes.summary: The text discusses multimedia data encoding, focusing on video and audio compression. It explains GOP issues in videoconferencing where B frames cause delays, suggesting motion-JPEG or GOPs without B frames like I P P P P I. It then covers MP3 audio compression, starting with CD-quality audio bit rates (1.41 Mbps) and telephone-quality (64 kbps), and the need for compression. MP3 uses three layers, with Layer III common. It employs subband splitting, block processing, DCT, quantization, and Huffman coding, with psychoacoustic models for bit allocation. Compressed subbands are framed with headers for decoding and interleaving. Finally, it summarizes presentation formatting (XDR, ASN.1, NDR, XML) and compression (JPEG, MPEG, MP3), noting lossy vs. lossless and evolving standards.

This section covers multimedia data compression and transmission. It introduces XML namespaces and multimedia's dominance of Internet traffic, contrasting lossless and lossy compression. Lossless techniques include Huffman, RLE, DPCM, delta encoding, and Lempel-Ziv. Image compression details JPEG's RGB to YUV conversion, chrominance subsampling, DCT, quantization, and encoding (30:1 ratios), plus GIF. Audio compression focuses on MP3's layers, subband splitting, psychoacoustic models, and Huffman coding. It concludes with presentation formatting (XDR, ASN.1, NDR, XML) and compression standard evolution.

nodes.title: 7.3 Summary
nodes.summary: The text explains audio frame packaging with headers for synchronization and bit allocation, interleaving with video frames, and the importance of not dropping audio frames during congestion. The chapter summary covers application data encoding in network packets, including presentation formatting (byte order, data structure linearization) and mechanisms like XDR, ASN.1, NDR, and XML, plus compression (lossless/lossy) for images, video, and audio (JPEG, MPEG, MP3). nodes.title: What’s Next: Video Everywhere
nodes.summary: The text discusses video as dominant Internet traffic with three-screen delivery, straining bandwidth and prompting new architectures like content-centric networking. It highlights challenges in converging video coding and streaming protocols across browsers and devices, including HTML5 codec patent conflicts. It addresses plug-and-play IP device configuration and home network management. Finally, it provides further reading on JPEG, MPEG, layered multicast, presentation formatting (XDR, ASN.1, NDR), compression (Huffman, LZ, Welch), and multimedia books.

nodes.title: Further Reading
nodes.summary: This text covers recommended readings and resources for end-to-end data topics. It highlights papers on JPEG and MPEG standards, receiver-driven layered multicast, and presentation formatting with performance issues. Compression references include Huffman, LZ algorithms, and multimedia books. Live references for XML and MPEG are provided. title: Chapter 8. Network Security

nodes.title: Problem: Security Attacks
nodes.summary: This text introduces network security, covering threats like eavesdropping, data tampering, replay attacks, DNS spoofing, website defacement, DoS attacks, and malicious code (worms, viruses, botnets). It defines security properties: confidentiality, traffic confidentiality, data integrity, originality, timeliness, authentication, access control, and availability. It notes the Internet's lack of built-in security and the need for patches. The chapter overview includes cryptographic building blocks (ciphers, hashes), key distribution, secure protocols, and current security systems, emphasizing cryptography's role.

nodes.title: 8.1 Cryptographic Building Blocks
8.1.1 Principles of Ciphers
nodes.summary: The text introduces cryptographic building blocks for network security. It discusses botnets and DoS attacks, then notes the Internet's original lack of security and the need for patches or redesign. It outlines tools like cryptography and firewalls, focusing on cryptographic methods. It covers cipher principles: encryption/decryption, key-based public algorithms, attacker knowledge (ciphertext-only, known-plaintext, chosen-plaintext), brute-force key search and key size, block ciphers, ECB weaknesses, and modes like CBC and counter mode. It defines symmetric-key ciphers, mentioning DES and NIST standards.

nodes.title: 8.1.2 Symmetric-Key Ciphers
nodes.summary: The text covers block ciphers, which encrypt fixed-size blocks, and their weakness in ECB mode where identical plaintext blocks yield identical ciphertext. It introduces modes of operation like CBC, which XORs each block with the previous ciphertext using an initialization vector, and counter mode. It then discusses symmetric-key ciphers, where both parties share the same secret key, detailing standards: DES with its 56-bit keys now vulnerable to brute force, Triple DES with 168-bit keys but slow and 64-bit blocks, and AES with key lengths of 128, 192, or 256 bits and 128-bit blocks, offering fast, secure implementation. Finally, it introduces public-key ciphers, which use a pair of keys: a private decryption key kept secret and a public encryption key shared openly.

nodes.title: 8.1.3 Public-Key Ciphers
nodes.summary: The text covers 3DES encryption/decryption using three DES keys, its slowness and 64-bit block limitations, and its replacement by AES (Rijndael) with 128/192/256-bit keys and 128-bit blocks. It introduces public-key ciphers, detailing key pairs, private/public keys, encryption/decryption, one-way channels, and authentication use. RSA, ElGamal, and elliptic curve cryptography are described, noting their reliance on hard math problems and large keys. Public-key ciphers are slower than symmetric ones, used for authentication and key distribution. Finally, authenticators are introduced for data integrity and authentication, referencing checksums and CRCs.

nodes.title: 8.1.4 Authenticators
nodes.summary: This text covers cryptographic building blocks: RSA and ElGamal public-key ciphers, their reliance on factoring and discrete logarithm problems, large key requirements, and elliptic curve cryptography. It notes public-key ciphers are slower than symmetric-key ciphers. Authenticators are introduced for data integrity and authentication, including cryptographic hash functions (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-2, SHA-3), message digests, digital signatures (DSS, RSA, ElGamal, ECDSA), and MACs/HMACs. It discusses collision and preimage attacks, birthday attacks, and combining authentication with confidentiality. Finally, it introduces key predistribution and session keys.

nodes.title: 8.2 Key predistribution
8.2 Key predistribution (intro)
nodes.summary: The text explains HMACs, where a hashed message authentication code is appended to a plaintext message, and only a receiver with the secret value can verify it. It discusses adding confidentiality by encrypting the message and its authenticator, often with symmetric-key ciphers, and notes that authenticators are foundational but not complete. It then introduces key predistribution, differentiating session keys from predistributed keys, and gives motivations for this division: limiting key usage time, predistribution issues, and speed trade-offs. It begins discussing public key predistribution and the need for a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) to certify key-identity bindings.

nodes.title: 8.2.1 Predistribution of Public Keys
8.2.1 Predistribution of Public Keys (intro)
nodes.summary: This section from Chapter 8 on Network Security discusses the rationale for separating session keys from predistributed keys, including limiting key usage to reduce attack exposure, the problem of predistributing symmetric keys, and the superiority of public key ciphers for authentication but not for bulk encryption. It introduces predistributed key distribution and future session key establishment, using Alice and Bob as participants. It then focuses on predistribution of public keys, explaining the need for a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) to certify key-identity bindings and the requirement for out-of-band identity verification.

nodes.title: 8.2 Key predistribution 649
nodes.summary: The text covers key predistribution and PKI bootstrapping, including out-of-band key exchange, digital signatures, certificates, and CAs. It explains how trust in a key can be extended via signed statements, enabling scalable key dissemination. It defines certificates as signed bindings of public keys to identities, describes the X.509 standard's required and optional components, and addresses the need for well-defined namespaces. It presents the certification authority model of trust, where binary trust and chains of certificates (often in a hierarchical tree) allow users to build trust from a known root key.

nodes.title: Certification Authorities
nodes.summary: This text covers digital signatures and certificate components, including optional expiration. It discusses identity in certificates, requiring well-defined namespaces like email or DNS. Two PKI trust models are presented: Certification Authorities (CAs), which use binary trust and hierarchical chains of trust, with issues like CA verification failures, X.509 restrictions, and multiple roots common in web browsers; and the Web of Trust, exemplified by PGP, where trust is decentralized, personal, and degree-based, with certificates including confidence levels and key-signing parties.

nodes.title: Web of Trust
nodes.summary: The text covers the web of trust model, exemplified by PGP, which uses a decentralized trust approach where individuals assign varying trust levels and confidence to certificates without CAs. It details PGP key-signing parties and certificate collection. Then, it addresses certificate revocation using CRLs, including expiration dates to manage list length. Finally, it introduces predistribution of symmetric keys, highlighting challenges: the need for N(N-1)/2 keys and the requirement to keep secret keys confidential.

nodes.title: Certificate Revocation

It notes that certificates have expiration dates to limit CRL growth. The text then introduces symmetric key predistribution, contrasting it with public keys: symmetric keys require N(N-1)/2 keys for N entities and must be kept secret, unlike public keys.

nodes.title: 8.2.2 Predistribution of Symmetric Keys
