nodes.title: 8.3 Authentication Protocols
8.3 Authentication Protocols (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers key distribution and authentication protocols in network security. It discusses using a Key Distribution Center (KDC) to reduce key management, mentioning Kerberos. It explains challenges in authentication protocols: replay and suppress-replay attacks affecting originality and timeliness, and session key establishment. The text notes authentication protocols often combine session key establishment, with Diffie-Hellman as an exception. It describes techniques for originality and timeliness: timestamps (requiring clock synchronization) and nonces (requiring tracking), and suggests combining them for efficiency.

nodes.title: 8.3.1 Originality and Timeliness Techniques
nodes.summary: The text discusses authentication protocols, focusing on the need for messages to be original and timely to be considered authentic. It explains that authentication protocols often establish session keys and are nearly synonymous with session key establishment protocols. It details originality and timeliness techniques: timestamps, which require clock synchronization and have accuracy limitations, and nonces, which require tracking past values. Combining timestamps and nonces or using challenge-response protocols addresses these issues, providing both timeliness and authentication. Challenge-response protocols are highlighted for their efficiency in proving timeliness without distributed clock synchronization. The text then transitions to public-key authentication protocols, assuming predistributed public keys via a PKI.

nodes.title: 8.3.2 Public-Key Authentication Protocols
nodes.summary: The text covers network authentication protocols. It explains challenge-response protocols using timestamps or nonces to combine timeliness and authentication, addressing clock synchronization issues. It then details public-key authentication protocols: one relying on synchronized clocks with timestamped, signed messages and session keys, and another not requiring synchronization, using timestamps as nonces. Finally, it introduces symmetric-key authentication protocols for larger systems using a Key Distribution Center (KDC), mentioning the Needham-Schroeder protocol where the KDC does not authenticate Alice's initial message or communicate with Bob.

nodes.title: 8.3.3 Symmetric-Key Authentication Protocols
8.3.3 Symmetric-Key Authentication Protocols (intro)
nodes.summary: This text covers network security authentication protocols. It begins with a timestamp-based public-key protocol where Alice and Bob verify freshness. It then details symmetric-key authentication, focusing on the Needham-Schroeder protocol involving Alice, Bob, and a Key Distribution Center (KDC), explaining nonces and session key distribution, and noting a flaw in Bob's freshness check. Finally, it introduces Kerberos, an evolution of Needham-Schroeder for client/server environments, which splits the KDC into an Authentication Server (AS) and a Ticket Granting Server (TGS) to minimize password exposure and enable multiple service tickets. It also mentions Kerberos's assumption of clock synchronization.

nodes.title: Kerberos
nodes.summary: The text covers network security authentication protocols, focusing on Kerberos and Diffie-Hellman. Kerberos, based on Needham-Schroeder, uses a KDC split into an Authentication Server (AS) and Ticket Granting Server (TGS) for client/server authentication, managing password exposure, and using timestamps due to clock synchronization. It supports cryptographic algorithms like SHA-1, MD5, AES, 3DES, and DES. Diffie-Hellman key agreement allows establishing a session key without pre-distributed keys, using public parameters p and g, but lacks authentication, often augmented, e.g., in IKE for IPsec.

This section covers symmetric-key authentication protocols, starting with a timestamp-based public-key protocol for freshness. It details the Needham-Schroeder protocol using a Key Distribution Center (KDC), nonces, and session key distribution, noting a flaw in freshness checking. It then introduces Kerberos, an evolution for client/server environments, which splits the KDC into an Authentication Server (AS) and a Ticket Granting Server (TGS) to minimize password exposure and enable multiple service tickets, assuming clock synchronization and supporting algorithms like SHA-1, MD5, AES, 3DES, and DES. Finally, it discusses Diffie-Hellman key agreement for session key establishment without pre-distributed keys, using public parameters p and g, but lacking authentication, often augmented in protocols like IKE for IPsec.

nodes.title: 8.3.4 Diffie--Hellman Key Agreement
nodes.summary: The text covers cryptographic algorithms (SHA-1, MD5, AES, 3DES, DES) and the Diffie–Hellman key agreement protocol, including its use of public parameters p and g, key exchange process, vulnerability to man-in-the-middle attacks, and the fixed variant with certificates for authentication. nodes.title: 8.4 Example systems

nodes.title: 8.4.1 Pretty Good Privacy (PGP)

nodes.title: 8.4.2 Secure Shell (SSH)
8.4.2 Secure Shell (SSH) (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers PGP email authentication, noting digital signatures authenticate senders but lack timeliness or originality proofs, while email characteristics suit one-message protocols. It then details Secure Shell (SSH), used for remote login, command execution, and file transfer, replacing Telnet and rlogin. SSH version 2 comprises SSH-TRANS (encrypted channel with RSA server authentication and session keys), SSH-AUTH (password, public-key, or host-based authentication), and SSH-CONN (connection protocol). The text discusses server key verification, key management, and SSH port forwarding for VPNs. Finally, it introduces Transport Layer Security (TLS/SSL/HTTPS) and its design goals for securing web transactions.

nodes.title: 8.4.3 Transport Layer Security (TLS, SSL, HTTPS)
nodes.summary: SSH port forwarding secures TCP applications like email via SSH tunnels, providing confidentiality, authentication, and potential VPNs. Transport Layer Security (TLS/SSL) addresses Web transaction needs for confidentiality, integrity, and authentication. TLS operates between application and TCP layers, enabling HTTPS. The handshake protocol negotiates cryptography: hash algorithms (MD5, SHA-1), symmetric ciphers (DES, 3DES, AES), session key establishment (Diffie-Hellman, RSA, DSS), and compression. It derives a 384-bit master secret from which six keys are generated for encryption and HMACs. Authentication can be mutual, server-only (common), or anonymous.

nodes.title: The Handshake Protocol
nodes.summary: This text covers TLS within network security, focusing on the Handshake and Record Protocols. The Handshake Protocol negotiates cryptographic algorithms (hash, cipher, key establishment, compression), establishes a master secret from a pre-master secret and nonces, and supports mutual, single, or no authentication. The Record Protocol provides confidentiality and integrity by fragmenting, optionally compressing, HMAC-protecting, and encrypting application data, using sequence numbers to prevent replays. TLS derives six keys from the master secret.

nodes.title: The Record Protocol
nodes.summary: The text covers TLS handshake completion, including server messages, client authentication, pre-master and master secret generation, and handshake verification to detect tampering. It details the TLS Record Protocol's steps: fragmentation, compression, HMAC integrity protection with sequence numbers to prevent replay, and encryption. It explains TLS session resumption as an optimization to avoid full handshakes for repeated connections. Finally, it introduces IPsec as a framework for IP-layer security, noting its optional status in IPv4 and mandatory in IPv6, and its modularity with three degrees of freedom.

nodes.title: 8.4.4 IP Security (IPsec)

nodes.title: 8.5 Firewalls

It then introduces firewalls as a non-cryptographic security measure against worms, viruses, and unpatched vulnerabilities. Firewalls sit at network boundaries, block traffic by default, and filter based on IP, TCP, and UDP information. They create zones of trust, including internal networks, DMZs, and the Internet, and can restrict outgoing traffic. Firewalls are often combined with NAT and may be implemented as appliances, routers, or personal firewalls.

nodes.title: 8.5 Firewalls 683
nodes.summary: Firewalls filter packets using rules with IP addresses and ports, including wildcards, and can be stateless or stateful, with modern ones filtering application-layer protocols. They may forward all except blocked packets or use a default-deny strategy, though misconfiguration is common. Firewalls provide centralized, unilateral protection but cannot secure legitimate communication, may be bypassed, and internal breaches or trusted external parties can introduce vulnerabilities.

nodes.title: 8.5.1 Strengths and Weaknesses of Firewalls

nodes.title: 8.6 Summary

nodes.title: 9.1 Traditional Applications
9.1 Traditional Applications (intro)
nodes.summary: The text discusses building networked applications using lower-layer protocols. It distinguishes application programs from protocols, noting standardized protocols enable interoperation. nodes.title: Message Format

nodes.title: Message Transfer

nodes.title: Mail Reader

nodes.title: 9.1.2 World Wide Web (HTTP)
9.1.2 World Wide Web (HTTP) (intro)

nodes.title: 9.1.3 Web Services
9.1.3 Web Services (intro)
nodes.summary: This chapter section covers web caching directives and CDNs, then introduces Web Services for direct application-to-application communication, driven by business needs. It explains two architectures: SOAP (WSDL and SOAP) and REST. SOAP uses WSDL for procedural protocol specification with operations, Message Exchange Patterns, XML Schema data models, and bindings. REST treats services as web resources accessed via HTTP. Both are actively adopted but lack empirical data on dominance.

nodes.title: Defining Application Protocols
nodes.summary: The text covers WSDL and SOAP for Web Services. It explains WSDL's procedural operation model, where abstract interfaces consist of operations (e.g., CheckAvailability), each specifying Message Exchange Patterns (MEPs) like In-Only and In-Out. MEPs are templates with placeholders for message formats defined via XML Schema. WSDL separates abstract definitions (operations, MEPs, message formats) from concrete bindings to protocols like HTTP and SOAP, with reusable modules across documents using XML namespaces. SOAP is presented as a framework for defining transport protocols, using XML Schema, bindings, MEPs, and reusable components to compose protocols with needed features.

nodes.title: Defining Transport Protocols
nodes.summary: WSDL modularity enables reuse of specification modules, with documents uniquely identified by XML namespaces and include/import mechanisms. SOAP acts as a framework for defining transport protocols via reusable components, feature abstraction (URI, state processing, relayed information, MEP lifecycles), and two implementation strategies: layering (e.g., HTTP binding) and header blocks/modules. SOAP message structure (Envelope, Header, Body) is shown, with modules composing features but risking interference. The text concludes that WSDL and SOAP are standards for specifying protocols, requiring enterprises to standardize specific protocols for interoperability.

nodes.title: Standardizing Web Services Protocols
nodes.summary: The text describes SOAP message structure with envelope, header, and body, and SOAP modules for composable protocol features, noting potential interference. It discusses standardizing Web Services protocols, highlighting WSDL and SOAP as standards, and the role of profiles like WS-I Basic Profile and Basic Security Profile in resolving choices and adding security. It introduces WS-Security and WS-* standards from OASIS, and contrasts the WSDL/SOAP architecture with the REST approach based on re-applying existing web principles.

nodes.title: A Generic Application Protocol (REST)

It covers WS-Security and WS-* standards from OASIS. It contrasts REST, which uses HTTP methods and document-passing, with WSDL/SOAP's customized protocols, noting REST's advantages in scalability, security, and evolvability, while SOAP may better wrap legacy applications. nodes.title: Domain Hierarchy
nodes.summary: The text discusses Internet naming, focusing on DNS. It contrasts the early flat hosts.txt table maintained by NIC with DNS's hierarchical namespace, distributed across name servers. DNS names are processed right-to-left with periods, unlike Unix file names. The domain hierarchy is a tree with top-level domains (original big six and newer ones, plus country codes) and supports non-Latin scripts. Name resolution translates domain names to IP addresses via a sequence of steps involving applications and name servers. The hierarchy is partitioned into zones for implementation.

nodes.title: Name Servers
nodes.summary: The text covers DNS domain hierarchy and implementation, including the 'big six' top-level domains, newer TLDs, and internationalized domain names. It explains zone partitioning and name servers, detailing resource record types (A, NS, CNAME, MX) and their fields (Name, Value, Type, Class, TTL). nodes.title: Name Resolution
nodes.summary: The text explains DNS infrastructure, covering MX records for email and CNAME for web server aliasing, and sample resource records. It details name resolution via root, TLD, and authoritative servers, bootstrap methods, local name server caching, and partial name handling. It outlines identifier levels: domain names, IP addresses, and physical addresses, with mappings via DNS and ARP. Finally, it introduces network management and SNMP, including GET, SET, and GET-NEXT operations.

nodes.title: 9.4 Overlay networks
9.4 Overlay networks (intro)

nodes.title: Overlays and the Ossification of the Internet
nodes.summary: The text discusses Internet ossification, where commercial interests and compatibility pressures hinder innovation and core infrastructure changes, as noted in a 2001 NRC report. It highlights the difficulty of introducing disruptive technologies like new routing strategies. Overlay networks are presented as a solution, allowing new capabilities via programmable nodes on conventional connectivity, with potential migration to base systems. Routing overlays are exemplified by VPNs using IP tunnels, and experimental systems for deploying new IP versions, such as the MBone for IP multicast, which used tunnels and a different forwarding algorithm.

nodes.title: 9.4.1 Routing Overlays
Experimental Versions of IP

It discusses experimental IP versions like the MBone for IP multicast and 6-BONE for IPv6 deployment, both using tunnels through legacy routers. End system multicast is presented as an alternative when IP multicast is not ubiquitous, where end hosts implement multicast trees via UDP tunnels, treating the Internet as a fully connected graph to find embedded multicast trees.

nodes.title: End System Multicast
nodes.summary: The text discusses overlay networks, focusing on 6-BONE for IPv6 deployment via tunnels, and end system multicast as an alternative to IP multicast. It details end system multicast's architecture, including mesh construction, membership management, and tree selection. It also covers maintaining the mesh through utility and cost evaluations, and introduces resilient overlay networks that exploit the triangle inequality not holding in the Internet to find alternative unicast routes.

nodes.title: Resilient Overlay Networks
nodes.summary: The text details overlay network mesh maintenance via utility and cost evaluation, and DVMRP multicast tree selection. It introduces Resilient Overlay Networks (RONs) exploiting triangle inequality violations by monitoring latency, bandwidth, and loss between pairs to find optimal routes and quickly recover from failures, though it scales only to dozens of nodes. It discusses RON's benefits and open scalability questions, highlights virtualization as a central concept, and begins introducing peer-to-peer networks like Napster and KaZaA.

Peer-to-peer networks allow users to pool resources without centralized coordination, though Napster was not fully peer-to-peer due to its central registry. nodes.title: Gnutella
nodes.summary: The text defines peer-to-peer networks as resource pooling among users for decentralized access, contrasting with Napster's central registry. It highlights decentralization, self-organization, and scalability, introducing overlay networks. Gnutella is examined as an early decentralized system using flooding queries with TTL, QIDs, and PING/PONG messages, discussing its graph evolution, limitations, and potential improvements like replication. Structured overlays are introduced as an alternative for reliable, efficient object location, contrasting with unstructured approaches.

nodes.title: Structured Overlays

It introduces structured overlays using consistent hashing to map objects and nodes onto an ID space, detailing routing, DHTs, Pastry's routing table and leaf set, node addition, and delay optimization. It then describes BitTorrent's piece replication, swarm lifecycle, and .torrent file-based joining.

nodes.title: BitTorrent

It details swarm lifecycle, piece exchange, peer IDs, tracker communication, and fairness via choking. Content Distribution Networks (CDNs) address web bottlenecks (first/last mile, server, peering points) by geographically distributing server surrogates to cache content, improving delivery.

9.4.3 Content Distribution Networks (intro)

CDNs use geographically distributed surrogate servers (caches) to replicate static content, handle flash crowds, and avoid peering issues.
